sections.title: FOREWORD
sections.html:
An important question that has divided Christians is whether the Sabbath law of the Ten Commandments is to be obeyed today by Christians. This is no small issue since our obedience to God's Word is at stake. In this very helpful and accessible book, Trey Talley argues that the Sabbath law of the Mosaic Covenant was to be obeyed by Israel under that covenant, but that in God's covenantal plan, the Sabbath was also revelatory as it pointed forward to greater rest achieved in Christ Jesus our Lord. In fact, now that Christ has come and ratified the New Covenant, the Sabbath command no longer applies to Christians as a covenantal obligation; instead, Christians are to "obey" the command in light of its fulfillment in Christ. In Christ's person and work, the Lord of Glory has perfectly obeyed all the demands of the covenant for us, paid for our sin, and secured salvation rest for his people. What Adam, and indeed humanity was created to enjoy in the beginning, namely covenantal relationship with the triune God, was lost in the Fall, recovered in type and shadow under the Old Covenant, but now in Christ is restored. Although the Church awaits the consummation of Christ's work in a new heavens and new earth where rest will be fully realized, even now we enter the salvation rest that our Lord has won for us. In truth, as Trey Talley rightly argues, to properly understand the Sabbath command in its place in redemptive history and how it is now fulfilled in Christ, is to better understand God's glorious plan of redemption from creation to the new creation. That is why if you want to better grasp something of the sweep of God's eternal plan centered in Christ and the good news of the Gospel, this book is for you. It works through the biblical data carefully, draws theological conclusions from the entirety of God's Word, and answers important questions with pastoral care and wisdom. I highly recommend this book for all Christians who want to think through the Sabbath debate, and especially for those who want to glory in our triune God of grace who accomplished our salvation rest in the New Covenant work of our Lord Jesus Christ."

Stephen J. Wellum, Ph.D., professor of Christian Theology at the Southern Baptist Theological Seminary, and author of God’s Kingdom through God’s Covenants.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION: CLOSED ON SUNDAY.
sections.html: When I was a child growing up in a rural town in Arkansas, no stores were open on Sundays. I remember asking my parents about this several times, to which I was simply told, "Because it is Sunday." You see, our town, like many towns at that time, had rules in place that prohibited businesses from being open on Sunday because it was the Sabbath day. This was just how it had always been and forever would be, or so I assumed. One day at the end of our Sunday worship service, the pastor announced that he had received word that our main grocery store would soon be allowed to open on Sundays. The congregation was shocked. People could not believe that such dreadful, ungodly activity was going to take place in our small, Christian town. Most churches condemned the action and warned their members not to support the grocery store’s "violation of the Sabbath" by shopping there on a Sunday. I can recall the first day that our city did away with the Sunday laws, and the store was allowed to be open at noon. Our church was located on Main Street, as was the grocery store. Our main entrance to the church was directly across from the grocery store, and we even shared the same parking lot. This gave us a bird’s eye view of anyone daring to violate the Sabbath day with their sinful shopping. Our worship service had just ended, and as usual, we made our way out of the building towards the parking lot. That is when I looked up and saw the unthinkable... cars at the grocery store. People were shopping on Sunday! I couldn't believe it. How could people so blatantly and openly sin? This controversy quickly became the talk of the town. Who would dare to sin against God in such a public manner, downtown on Main Street for everyone to see? Well, as months went by, the town slowly accepted the changes, the sermons about violating the Sabbath stopped, and the talk of who the sinners were that were buying groceries ceased. I even found myself being told by my parents to run into the grocery store after church to grab a carton of milk. As years went by, what had been considered an abomination before God, was now regular activity for our town, church, and family. Instead of our church looking at those going in and out of the grocery store on Sunday as sinful God-haters, we were now standing in line with them. So, the question is, “Which view of Sunday was correct.” Did I sin when I bought a carton of milk from the store on Sunday? Or, for further thought, were the employees of the grocery store sinning by working on Sunday? Did our church and our town think rightly about the "Sabbath" by keeping all stores closed or by allowing them to be open? As long ago as that was, I continued to wonder about the Sabbath day controversy many times in my life. I have found that I am not alone. The Sunday dilemma requires a clear solution. Some Scriptures forbid work on the Sabbath and even command such a person to be put to death. So, are those Scriptures still applicable? Is it a sin to work on Sunday? Many people, churches, and entire theological systems weigh in quite differently. Hopefully and prayerfully, this book will help you to gain clarity on such issues and to increase your understanding of what it means to truly have Sabbath rest.

sections.title: CHAPTER 1: WHEN WAS THE SABBATH COMMAND GIVEN?
sections.html:
To understand the Sabbath, it is of utmost importance to establish when God first commanded people to honor the Sabbath. There are two competing views on when God commanded the prohibition of working on the Sabbath. Some believe that the Sabbath was given to mankind as early as the seventh day of creation, and others believe that God did not give the Sabbath command until He descended upon Mt. Sinai. Choosing the correct start date for the Sabbath may seem like a minor issue to some, but, as we will see, the choice of a Genesis or an Exodus timing of the Sabbath command creates a tremendous theological difference. Those who adhere to the Genesis start date of the Sabbath believe that God commanded mankind to honor the Sabbath on the seventh day of creation. This view is held by churches that adhere to Covenant Theology.1 Are they correct? Let’s begin by examining the primary passage from which they draw to see if such a conclusion can be reached.

Thus the heavens and the earth were finished, and all the host of them. And on the seventh day, God finished his work that he had done, and he rested on the seventh day from all his work that he had done. So God blessed the seventh day and made it holy, because on it God rested from all his work that he had done in creation. (Genesis 2:1-3)

So, does this passage prove an early Genesis Sabbath command origination date? Does God's completion of His work of creation on day seven mean that it doubled as a command that prohibited Adam, Eve, and all humanity, from ever working on day seven? What truths can be gained from this passage? One could arrive at the fact that God completed His work of creation on day six and rested on day seven. I believe one could even conclude that Adam and Eve were to find their rest in God's provision for them. In Genesis 2, we read of the beauty of the Garden of Eden, where Adam and Eve enjoyed plentiful water, food, and ease of work. However, there was no command for Adam and Eve to refrain from work on the seventh day ever mentioned. There is also – and this is very important – no divine command in the creation account of Genesis to set apart the seventh day as a special day of sacrifice or worship. The existence of a seventh day in creation does not imply, much less establish, a moral and legal obligation. As pastor and theologian, Blake White has written:

It is one thing to say that the seventh day of creation set the precedent and basis for the later commandment; It is quite another to turn a foundation into a command. Christian teachers ought to have clear textual warrant to turn an indicative into an imperative. A command to obey the Sabbath is nowhere grounded in the created order.2

SABBATH SILENCE

In fact, not only is such a command absent from the creation narrative, but it is also absent from the entire book of Genesis. The book of Genesis is a lengthy book covering over a 1000-year history of the first humans. However, we have no evidence that anyone held the seventh day as a special day of rest. The silence of the book of Genesis regarding the Sabbath never being commanded by God or kept by man is no small matter. If God had revealed that such a day was connected to the creation, then Moses, the author of the book of Genesis and the "law giver," would surely have mentioned it. However, there is no mention of the Sabbath being commanded or kept by anyone in the book of Genesis. Why? Because God had not commanded anyone to do so. Think of all the people who are mentioned in the book of Genesis. Think about all the life details recorded for us in Genesis, yet there is no mention of anyone ever keeping the Sabbath or breaking the Sabbath. The Sabbath silence of the book of Genesis is an insurmountable mountain for those who strive to prove that mankind was commanded to keep the Sabbath from creation. In the book of Genesis, Moses recorded Abraham's life story, from Abraham being called by God to his death. Yet nothing is ever mentioned about Abraham keeping or breaking the Sabbath. God even made a covenant with Abraham, yet nowhere in the covenant is keeping the Sabbath ever mentioned or commanded by God.3 The same silence regarding the Sabbath can be also said of his son Isaac, his grandson Jacob, and his great-grandsons. Consider Abraham’s grandson Joseph. We have fourteen chapters of detailed information about the life of Joseph, yet no mention of Joseph keeping or breaking the Sabbath. Long story short, from Adam and Eve (the very first humans) to all of those who followed: Cain, Abel, Seth, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, no one was ever recorded as treating the seventh day of the week any differently than the other days of the week. Why is there no mention of the Sabbath? Because clearly, God had not yet given it as a command to be kept. So, if there is no Sabbath command in the entire history of mankind that Genesis covers, then when does God give the Sabbath command? The Sabbath silence of Genesis compels us to look to a later time for the giving of the command. Where do we look? The book of Exodus. The book of Exodus is the opposite of silence regarding the Sabbath. In fact, by comparison, it shouts and gives us absolute clarity as to when God gave the Sabbath command.

THE SABBATH IS ANNOUNCED

As you know, the book of Exodus opens with the people of Israel in Egyptian slavery. God calls Moses to go to the Pharaoh and demand that the Israelites be set free. Finally, after God sends ten plagues upon Egypt, the Pharaoh lets the Israelites go free. God removes the Israelites from Egypt and takes them out to the desert. It is at this time that we have the first mention of a Sabbath day rest being commanded by God. It occurred when Israel was hungry, and God supernaturally provided food for them.

On the sixth day, they gathered twice as much bread, two omers each. And when all the leaders of the congregation came and told Moses, he said to them, "This is what the LORD has commanded: 'Tomorrow is a day of solemn rest, a holy Sabbath to the LORD; bake what you will bake and boil what you will boil, and all that is left over lay aside to be kept till the morning.'" So they laid it aside till the morning, as Moses commanded them, and it did not stink, and there were no worms in it. Moses said, "Eat it today, for today is a Sabbath to the LORD; today you will not find it in the field. Six days you shall gather it, but on the seventh day, which is a Sabbath, there will be none." On the seventh day some of the people went out to gather, but they found none. And the LORD said to Moses, "How long will you refuse to keep my commandments and my laws? See! The LORD has given you the Sabbath; therefore on the sixth day he gives you bread for two days. Remain each of you in his place; let no one go out of his place on the seventh day." So the people rested on the seventh day. (Exodus 16:22-30)

Here we have the explicit, first mention of a commandment not to work (gather food) on the seventh day of the week along with the command to stay home. This passage shows that the people now were to treat the seventh day differently from all other days. There is nothing in the text to draw any conclusion that they knew this command beforehand and were just now beginning to start the habit again. This Sabbath command of God to Israel in Exodus is a new command from God. This Sabbath command to stay home and cease from work was given to the Israelites as a precursor to the Sabbath rules that would soon be given as part of the covenant God would make with them. Soon, God called Moses to the top of Mt. Sinai and gave the terms of the covenant, which included the Sabbath regulations: Six days you shall labor, and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God. On it you shall not do any work, you, or your son, or your daughter, your male servant, or your female servant, or your livestock, or the sojourner who is within your gates. (Exodus 20:9-10) What does this mean? God did not give the Sabbath commands in Genesis, but in Exodus. There is no mention of anyone ever keeping the Sabbath day in Genesis because such a command did not exist. God clearly gave the Sabbath command to Israel at Mt. Sinai. The origination of the Sabbath command on Mt. Sinai can be further substantiated from the explicit statements provided by the prophets: So I led them out of the land of Egypt and brought them into the wilderness. I gave them my statutes and made known to them my rules, by which, if a person does them, he shall live. Moreover, I gave them my Sabbaths, as a sign between me and them, that they might know that I am the LORD who sanctifies them. But the house of Israel rebelled against me in the wilderness. They did not walk in my statutes but rejected my rules, by which, if a person does them, he shall live; and my Sabbaths they profaned. (Ezekiel 20:10-13) If we allow Scripture to speak and the words of Ezekiel to remain untainted from theological presuppositions, then it will tell us when God gave the Sabbath commands. God said that it was when "I led them out of the land of Egypt." God stated precisely when the Sabbath commands were given. God's own words through Ezekiel should remove any and all doubt as to when the command to keep the Sabbaths was given. God also spoke again, through the prophet Nehemiah, and clearly announced when He gave the Sabbath commands: You came down on Mount Sinai and spoke with them from heaven and gave them right rules and true laws, good statutes and commandments, and you made known to them your holy Sabbath and commanded them commandments and statutes and a law by Moses your servant. (Nehemiah 9:13-14) According to Nehemiah, when did God give the Sabbath commandments? The passage provides the time stamp, not at creation but on Mt. Sinai. God made known to Moses all that pertained to keeping the Sabbath day holy. This scene begs the question to those who hold that mankind was commanded to honor the Sabbath since the creation, "Why would God need to make known something that was already known?" If this were a command since the world’s creation, then God would not have to make it known to the Israelites. The concept of keeping the Sabbath was new information that was given to Israel at Mt. Sinai as recorded for us in Exodus. Summary: As a Christian, who or what is your ultimate source of authority for what you believe? Obviously, the correct answer is God and His word. This being the case, we have seen that God's word emphatically states the time of the giving of the Sabbath. God has spoken, and to go against His revelation is not wise. So, as we begin this study, it is important to note the silence of Genesis, and the voice of Exodus, Ezekiel, Nehemiah, and God about the timing of the giving of the Sabbath. This is in perfect accord with Paul’s teaching that the Law (which included the Sabbath), did not come until 430 years after Abraham.4 Why is it important to know when God gave the Sabbath command? First, because it is Biblical truth breathed out by God. Second, if people accept theology not rooted in Scripture, they can exalt theological systems as having more authority than God’s Word. Third, if you don't know when the Sabbath was given, it will lead to tremendous confusion as you seek to understand your response to the Old Covenant Sabbath regulations.

1 Covenant Theology is a framework for interpreting Scripture most commonly held by those who hold to the Westminster Confession of Faith and the 1689 Second London Baptist Confession of Faith. While both confessions contain much truth, I believe that they both share a common weakness in their view of the Sabbath.

2 A. Blake White, Obey the Sabbath: Rest in Christ (Abilene, TX: Canon Sense, 2020), 32.

3 Genesis 15,17: All Bible references are from The Holy Bible: English Standard Version Containing the Old and New Testaments: ESV. (Wheaton, Il: Crossway, 2011)

4 Galatians 3:16-17

sections.title: CHAPTER 2: WHO WAS COMMANDED TO KEEP THE SABBATH?
sections.html:
The first people ever commanded by God to keep the Sabbath was the nation of Israel when God gave them the rules for gathering manna.5 As mentioned in the last chapter, we do not have any Biblical record of any other humans being told to keep the Sabbath. The earlier command of God to only gather manna for six days was strictly given to those who had come out of slavery from Egypt.6 There is no Biblical record of God previously telling anyone but the Israelites who had been set free from Egypt to take the seventh day off from gathering food. We can also conclude that this was a new command. The Israelites had to be told not to gather food on the Sabbath because this was a new revelation from God. There is no Biblical record that God had ever commanded them or anyone else in human history to abstain from gathering food before that day in the desert. The day off from gathering manna was a precursor to establishing the Sabbath given to them upon their arrival at Mount Sinai. There is no Biblical record of any of the patriarchs of Israel ever receiving a command from God to honor the Sabbath as the Israelites were commanded to do so when God made His covenant with them. Nor is there any record of the patriarchs treating the seventh day differently from the rest. Moses makes this point to the Israelites right before he lists the Ten Commandments:

The LORD our God made a covenant with us in Horeb. Not with our fathers did the LORD make this covenant, but with us, who are all of us here alive today. (Deuteronomy 5:2-3)

Who the covenant was made with and not made with is a crucial point that must not be overlooked. God did not make this covenant with the Israelites’ ancestors; God specifically made it with Moses and the other Israelites who had been set free from Egypt. Along with this covenant came the sign of the covenant, the Sabbath, which was also unique to them.

Therefore the people of Israel shall keep the Sabbath, observing the Sabbath throughout their generations, as a covenant forever. It is a sign forever between me and the people of Israel that in six days the LORD made heaven and earth, and on the seventh day he rested and was refreshed. (Exodus 31:16-17)

The Sabbath was a sign explicitly given to Israel, the people with whom God was making a covenant. No one else before this moment was included in this covenant or given the sign of the covenant. Nor was there anyone else on earth included in this covenant or given the sign that accompanied it. God made the same point, but in a slightly different way, when He gave further instructions for the people to follow on the Sabbath day in Deuteronomy:

You shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God brought you out from there with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm. Therefore the LORD your God commanded you to keep the Sabbath day. (Deuteronomy 5:15)

The sign of the covenant, the Sabbath, was not given to anyone before the Exodus because those who came before them would not even have a reason to honor it yet. Israel, a slave nation, observed the Sabbath by remembering that Egypt had enslaved them, but God had supernaturally delivered them. On Mount Sinai, God made a covenant agreement with one nation, the nation of Israel. At this time, the Sabbath became more than a command not to gather manna, but the covenant sign between God and the people of Israel. The covenant and the sign of the covenant were exclusively for them. This point can easily be seen when we allow Scripture to speak for itself. For example, read over the giving of the Sabbath in Exodus 31, and you can't help but see that God gave the Sabbath to Israel.

And the LORD said to Moses, "You are to speak to the people of Israel and say, 'Above all you shall keep my Sabbaths, for this is a sign between me and you throughout your generations, that you may know that I, the LORD, sanctify you. You shall keep the Sabbath, because it is holy for you. Everyone who profanes it shall be put to death. Whoever does any work on it, that soul shall be cut off from among his people. Six days shall work be done, but the seventh day is a Sabbath of solemn rest, holy to the LORD. Whoever does any work on the Sabbath day shall be put to death. Therefore the people of Israel shall keep the Sabbath, observing the Sabbath throughout their generations, as a covenant forever. It is a sign forever between me and the people of Israel that in six days the LORD made heaven and earth, and on the seventh day he rested and was refreshed.'" (Exodus 31:12-17)

According to the passage, who is commanded to keep the Sabbath? It is impossible to come away from Deuteronomy 5 and Exodus 31 with any answer other than "Israel." God specifically states that "Israel shall keep the Sabbath." Why does God command the people of Israel to honor this day of rest? God is not ambiguous with His reasoning. He very clearly states that, "It is a sign forever between me and the people of Israel."7 It is also worth mentioning that God explained what it meant to honor this sign. They were to work six days and to rest on the seventh. God revealed to Israel what the Sabbath was and how it was to be observed. These commands did not serve as a reminder of what everyone in the world always knew to be true. Nor was it a reminder to the Israelites about the information they knew but had forgotten. This was brand new information that was part of God’s covenant between Himself and Israel. It is also important to address that a mention of creation accompanies the new Sabbath information that God is giving them. However, we must be careful not to read more into this than what was meant. Covenant theologians will say that the mention of God's work of six days followed by a day of rest is proof that the Sabbath command had always been God's law to all of mankind since creation. However, that is way more information than the text provides. The Bible is silent regarding any command for seventh day rest until the giving of the manna and later, the giving of the Sabbath as the covenant sign to Israel. God does not say anything in Exodus 31 or Deuteronomy 5, even resembling a worldwide universal Sabbath day command. The command is only given to Israel. The "rest" that God was giving Israel as a gift and a sign was analogous to God’s rest in Genesis after He made creation. On day seven, God rested from His work of creation, and the Israelites were to do so as well. This day of rest was to be a tremendous blessing for the people. They were no longer under the ruthless Pharaoh who worked them relentlessly; now, they were under the authority of a compassionate God who commanded them to refrain from work and rest in His provision. In addition, as we will see, the Sabbath was not only a gift to Israel, but it also functioned as a type or pattern that pointed forward to a greater rest to come. Summary: So, who was commanded to keep the Sabbath? The Bible gives no information of any other nation, people, or person ever being commanded to treat the seventh day differently than any other day until after the Exodus. The first people to receive any special command regarding the seventh day of the week was Israel. The first instruction was to cease work on the Sabbath pertaining to gathering manna, and later God commanded them to cease work as a sign of the Mosaic Covenant. In short, the Sabbath was not given to all of humanity since the time of Adam. Nor is the Sabbath part of God’s unchanging moral law for all of humanity to honor. Instead, the Biblical record reveals the Sabbath command was given as a sign for those under the Old Covenant. As we will see in the coming chapters, this fact has tremendous ramifications for those who consider themselves modern-day Sabbatarians, such as those who follow Covenant Theology.8

6 Exodus 16:1-5

7 Exodus 31:13

8 Sabbatarianism is the belief that the Sabbath is part of God’s unchanging moral law that was given at the time of creation and that all people must continue to observe even today.

sections.title: CHAPTER 3: HOW MANY SABBATHS?
sections.html:
In Exodus 31, God said, “Above all you shall keep my Sabbaths.”9 Why is the word Sabbath in the plural? What many people fail to realize is that God had commanded not only a Sabbath every seven days, but God had also commanded many other Sabbaths to be observed as well. For starters, additional Sabbath days coincided with the Passover, Feast of Firstfruits, Feast of Weeks, Feast of Trumpets, The Day of Atonement, and the Feast of Booths. God commanded all these days to be equally observed as Sabbath days of rest. Even if they were not on the seventh day, each special day was still treated as a sabbath.10 This can be seen by the command that accompanies the regulations for the Feast of Booths:

On the eighth day you shall hold a holy convocation and present a food offering to the LORD. It is a solemn assembly; you shall not do any ordinary work. (Leviticus 23:36)

In addition to the weekly Sabbaths and the six other special Sabbaths each year, there was also an entire year of Sabbath rest to be observed every seven years. As with the other Sabbaths, the yearly Sabbath came with rules and regulations for the Israelites to follow.

The LORD spoke to Moses on Mount Sinai, saying, “Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When you come into the land that I give you, the land shall keep a Sabbath to the LORD. For six years you shall sow your field, and for six years you shall prune your vineyard and gather in its fruits, but in the seventh year there shall be a Sabbath of solemn rest for the land, a Sabbath to the LORD. You shall not sow your field or prune your vineyard. You shall not reap what grows of itself in your harvest or gather the grapes of your undressed vine. It shall be a year of solemn rest for the land. The Sabbath of the land shall provide food for you, for yourself and for your male and female slaves and for your hired worker and the sojourner who lives with you, and for your cattle and for the wild animals that are in your land: all its yield shall be for food. (Leviticus 25:1-7)

Whether it was the Sabbath that occurred every seventh day, the Sabbath days that were to accompany the annual feasts, or the Sabbath year, all were equally a part of God’s law to the Israelites. They came from the same source, and to violate any of God’s Sabbaths was to be in sin.

CHOOSING JUST ONE?

Today, many people who feel the need to observe the weekly Sabbath violate Sabbath law by not observing the other Sabbaths prescribed by God. How can this be when all the Sabbaths have come with the same authority, to the same people, by the same God? If people arbitrarily choose which Sabbaths to keep, they must Biblically prove why some Sabbaths remain and others do not. Just

th

because the other Sabbaths were not mentioned in the 4 Commandment did not make them less of a law for Israel. God did not view certain Sabbaths as optional and others as mandatory. From a Biblical perspective, there appear to be only two choices for people today: to accept all of the Sabbaths as ongoing for God's covenant people or to see them all fulfilled by Christ's provision in salvation. Did Christ somehow fulfill the other Sabbaths, making them obsolete, yet not fulfill the seventh-day Sabbath? This is an intriguing problem for the adherents of Covenant Theology, who emphasize adherence to only the weekly Sabbath and dismiss all others. To violate any of the Sabbaths was a sin against God. A perfect example of this can be seen by looking at the history of Israel. They had continued to honor the weekly Sabbaths but had stopped honoring the seven-year Sabbaths that God had commanded them to keep. Did God view this as acceptable? Did Israel have the right to choose which Sabbath they would or would not keep? Would God not be as strict regarding his command to take a Sabbath every seven years? No, they went from a people receiving the blessings of God living in the promised land to a people receiving the wrath of God ejected from the promised land. Due to them not keeping the Sabbath every seventh year, God caused another nation to invade them and take them into slavery.

Therefore he brought up against them the king of the Chaldeans, who killed their young men with the sword in the house of their sanctuary and had no compassion on young man or virgin, old man or aged. He gave them all into his hand. And all the vessels of the house of God, great and small, and the treasures of the house of the LORD, and the treasures of the king and of his princes, all these he brought to Babylon. And they burned the house of God and broke down the wall of Jerusalem and burned all its palaces with fire and destroyed all its precious vessels. He took into exile in Babylon those who had escaped from the sword, and they became servants to him and to his sons until the establishment of the kingdom of Persia, to fulfill the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah, until the land had enjoyed its Sabbaths. All the days that it lay desolate it kept Sabbath, to fulfill seventy years. (2 Chronicles 36:17-21)

This passage teaches that God commanded the Israelites to observe all the Sabbaths. Apparently, the people had enough faith to believe that God would provide for them on the weekly Sabbaths and various annual Sabbaths, but they doubted God could provide for them if they honored the Sabbath year as God had prescribed. Their violation of the seven-year Sabbath was such a rebellion against God that He caused the ungodly nation of Babylon to wage war on them. God used Babylon to be the agent of His wrath against Israel for not obeying His commands to honor the seventh-year Sabbath. And to further remove any doubt as to why they were receiving the wrath of God, 2 Chronicles 36 lets us know that Israel’s 70-year punishment was because they did not follow God’s commands regarding the seven-year Sabbaths. Another point that is overlooked in this passage is that God used Babylon, a nation that worshipped other gods and who had never kept a single Sabbath, to conquer a nation that had at least honored some of the Sabbaths. If God gave the Sabbaths to all mankind, then God would have held Babylon more accountable than Israel since they never honored any Sabbaths in their nation’s history. But God’s punishment of only Israel makes perfect sense when we realize the Sabbaths had not been given to all of mankind, including the nation of Babylon. The Sabbath commands were directly assigned to, and only to, the nation of Israel. Summary: Scripture reveals that God gave more Sabbaths than just the seventh-day Sabbath. However, modern-day Sabbatarians have rejected the other Sabbaths. On what basis can this be done? All Sabbaths are part of the law that God gave Israel, and to neglect any of the Sabbaths was a violation of the law of God. My point is that those who want to bring the Old Covenant Sabbath forward into the New Covenant era should be consistent. There is no Biblical warrant to bring only one Sabbath forward at the neglect of the others. The same God who commanded the one also commanded the others, and the same law that contains the weekly Sabbath commands also includes the other Sabbaths. To be clear, I am not advocating for all Sabbaths to be observed by modern Christians. However, I want to expose the inconsistency of those who call themselves Sabbatarian yet do not observe all of the Sabbaths. To be consistent, they must equally observe all of the Sabbaths as they were prescribed, or none of the Sabbath days and years are to be observed. Again, we must consider who they were given to, why they were given, under which covenant they were given, and what that means to us in the New Covenant era.

sections.title: CHAPTER 4: HOW MUCH WORK WAS ALLOWED ON THE SABBATH?
sections.html:
Perhaps you have heard modern-day Sabbatarians justify a little work here and there as being permissible. However, the Bible would undoubtedly find such an Israelite in violation of the Sabbath. Whether it was a little work, a lot of work, or doing something to cause others to work, all such work was a sin. Consider the clarity of these Sabbath day regulations:

Six days shall work be done, but on the seventh day is a Sabbath of solemn rest, a holy convocation. You shall do no work. It is a Sabbath to the LORD in all your dwelling places. (Leviticus 23:3) Whoever does any work on it, that soul shall be cut off from among his people. Six days shall work be done, but the seventh day is a Sabbath of solemn rest, holy to the LORD. Whoever does any work on the Sabbath day shall be put to death. (Exodus 31:15)

How much work were the covenant people allowed to perform on the Sabbath? Obviously, the answer is "None." According to God’s regulations (laws), “no work” was to be done. The rule was straightforward and simple. Any work had to be done before or after, but the entire covenant community (Israel) was to cease working on the Sabbath. In the Sabbath regulations given by God, there are no excuses or justifications given in which anyone would be permitted to work. There was a “0 tolerance policy” in place. Whether it was a little or a lot, those who chose to work on the Sabbath broke the law and were to be put to death. Further clarity of God’s Sabbath prohibition of work is given in Deuteronomy:

Observe the Sabbath day, to keep it holy, as the LORD your God commanded you. Six days you shall labor and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God. On it you shall not do any work, you or your son or your daughter or your male servant or your female servant, or your ox or your donkey or any of your livestock, or the sojourner who is within your gates, that your male servant and your female servant may rest as well as you. (Deuteronomy 5:12-15)

The Lord added more stringency to the Sabbath command rest to ensure that some industriously minded person did not try to "keep" the Sabbath by getting others to do his work for him. Therefore, God gave Israel detailed instructions prohibiting them from having their children, servants, visitors, and even their animals from doing any work on the Sabbath. If the Israelites were not personally working, but reaping the benefits of having others work for them, they were still not truly resting in God because they were using others to violate the Sabbath on their behalf. It is also worth mentioning that along with God forbidding work to be done on the Sabbath, He also commanded work to be done on the other six days of the week. This command does not mean that the people were to labor all six days only if they needed to get their work done. Instead, they were commanded to work six days and only take off on the Sabbath day. Israel's time of work and time away from work were equally a part of the Sabbath commands. The line of demarcation was obvious, six days of work followed by one day of rest. The Israelites had to complete all work during the six days, and no work was to be done on the Sabbath.

STICKS AND STONES

What if someone decided to get most of their work done during the six days and do a little on the Sabbath? Soon after God had given the Sabbath commands, one such man did exactly that, forcing Moses to ask God what should be done as a punishment. Is the man to receive a verbal warning? A mild reprimand, or what? Well, from the passage, we find out that anyone caught working on the Sabbath was to be severely punished.

While the people of Israel were in the wilderness, they found a man gathering sticks on the Sabbath day. And those who found him gathering sticks brought him to Moses and Aaron and all the congregation. They put him in custody because it had not been made clear what should be done to him. And the LORD said to Moses, "The man shall be put to death; all the congregation shall stone him with stones outside the camp." And all the congregation brought him outside the camp and stoned him to death with stones, as the LORD commanded Moses. (Numbers 15:32-36)

The man who picked up sticks was put to death. Why would the simple task of picking up sticks warrant the same penalty as murder? We must remember that there is nothing wrong with picking up sticks in and of itself. That is unless it was done on the day when God had forbidden work to be done. The Sabbath was more than just a religious day; it was a day that God had set apart from the rest of the week to be the sign of the covenant between Himself and Israel. For a person to disregard God's commandments for the Sabbath was to reject the covenant sign and to reject God Himself. The man in Numbers 15 had openly rejected God by rejecting God's Covenant Sign. For such a sin, no sacrifice could be made for atonement. This Sabbath violator was given as an example, just after God had given the instructions for dealing with someone who sins with such a high-handed deliberate rebellion against God.

"If one person sins unintentionally, he shall offer a female goat a year old for a sin offering. And the priest shall make atonement before the LORD for the person who makes a mistake, when he sins unintentionally, to make atonement for him, and he shall be forgiven. You shall have one law for him who does anything unintentionally, for him who is native among the people of Israel and for the stranger who sojourns among them. But the person who does anything with a high hand, whether he is native or a sojourner, reviles the LORD, and that person shall be cut off from among his people. Because he has despised the word of the LORD and has broken his commandment, that person shall be utterly cut off; his iniquity shall be on him." (Numbers 15:27-31)

This passage immediately precedes the section explaining the death penalty for the man who violated the Sabbath. Breaking the Sabbath was an example of a high-handed sin. The man who was caught working on the Sabbath was openly and proudly rejecting the covenant. Such a person was to be "utterly cut off," and his "iniquity shall be on him." When God commanded that no work be done on the Sabbath, He literally meant "no work." The rules to abstain from work on the Sabbath were extremely clear, and there was no wiggle room whatsoever. The death of the man who picked up sticks was an example to all Israelites that God truly meant what He had said about honoring the sign of the covenant. The Sabbath was given to people as a blessing. Previously, while they were in slavery, they had to work as slaves, with no days off, but their new King commanded them to take time off. The Sabbath was both a sign and a gift from God for the covenant community. The people were to faithfully rest in God, and every Sabbath was one more opportunity to practically do so by trusting in God’s provision for them. Summary: What about you? Have you ever picked up a stick on the Sabbath or done other work? Have you ever had to work at your vocation on a Sabbath? Have you ever allowed your job to come home with you, where you accomplished some of your work on the Sabbath? Or perhaps you have cooked, cleaned, done the laundry, or mowed the yard on a Sabbath. If you answered "Yes," to any of the questions above, does this mean that you now deserve to die? Likewise, have you ever violated the Sabbath by causing others to work for you? For instance, have you ever gone to a grocery store on the Sabbath and, by doing so, caused others to violate the Sabbath? Have you ever gone to a restaurant on the Sabbath and, by doing so, caused others to cook and clean (work) so that you would not work on the Sabbath? If so, according to Deuteronomy 5, you have violated the Sabbath. Does this mean that you should be put to death? Before you get worried, let me jump ahead in the book a bit and say, "No, you should not be put to death." But why not? Honestly, why not? What one reason would you give a mob of people armed with rocks and the passages that we just went over, who caught you eating out at a restaurant on the Sabbath, not to kill you? Many Christians would seriously struggle to answer such a question. They all seem to know that they shouldn't be put to death but don't know why. The correct answer is that God gave the Sabbaths as part of a covenant to a particular people for a specific time. You should not be stoned for working on the Sabbath because God did not give those Sabbath rules to you, and along with that, neither were the punishments for breaking those Sabbath rules. The time of the Old Covenant has passed, and now believers are under a New Covenant that is superior to the Mosaic Covenant. As we will see, the Sabbath days and years of rest were a shadow of the ultimate rest that God provides by the Person and work of Jesus Christ.

sections.title: CHAPTER 5: WHAT DOES THE SABBATH HAVE TO DO WITH CIRCUMCISION?
sections.html:
While the observation of the Sabbath and the act of circumcision are different, they are also similar. Both are signs of covenants made between God and His people. Circumcision was given to Abraham and his lineage as a sign of the Abrahamic Covenant.11 The Sabbath was given to Moses and Israel as a sign of the Mosaic Covenant.12 God commanded His people to honor these signs. How serious was God about honoring the signs of the covenants? If an Israelite were not circumcised or worked on the Sabbath, he could be put to death. However, these two covenant signs also have something else in common: God no longer requires either of them. Why? Because under the New Covenant, both have been fulfilled by the Person and work of the Messiah in the salvation of His people. But, before we get too far ahead, let's look back to when God gave circumcision as a sign of the covenant that He was making with Abraham. As we will see, circumcision, like the Sabbath, was not given to mankind from creation, but it was given at a specific time for a particular people. In his summary of Jewish history, Stephen says that the sign of circumcision began in conjunction with the Abrahamic Covenant. Speaking of that interaction between Abraham and God, Stephen says:

And he gave him the covenant of circumcision. And so Abraham became the father of Isaac, and circumcised him on the eighth day, and Isaac became the father of Jacob, and Jacob of the twelve patriarchs. (Acts 7:8)

From this, it is easy to see that circumcision was not a sign given since creation. Like the Sabbath, it had a starting point. Not only did it have a specific starting point, but it also was for a specific people, the household of Abraham:

And God said to Abraham, "As for you, you shall keep my covenant, you and your offspring after you throughout their generations. This is my covenant, which you shall keep, between me and you and your offspring after you: Every male among you shall be circumcised. You shall be circumcised in the flesh of your foreskins, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and you. He who is eight days old among you shall be circumcised. Every male throughout your generations, whether born in your house or bought with your money from any foreigner who is not of your offspring, both he who is born in your house and he who is bought with your money, shall surely be circumcised. So shall my covenant be in your flesh an everlasting covenant. Any uncircumcised male who is not circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin shall be cut off from his people; he has broken my covenant." (Genesis 17:9-14)

This passage clarifies that circumcision was the covenant sign between God and Abraham's household. If anyone rejected the covenant sign, they would be removed from God's covenant people. The severity of breaking this command is seen by recalling the time when God almost put Moses to death:

At a lodging place on the way the LORD met him and sought to put him to death. Then Zipporah took a flint and cut off her son's foreskin and touched Moses' feet with it and said, "Surely you are a bridegroom of blood to me!" So he let him alone. It was then that she said, "A bridegroom of blood," because of the circumcision. (Exodus 4:24-26)

We are not given much to work with from this passage, but one thing is clear, Moses was guilty of not placing the sign of the covenant upon his son. It is hard to imagine, but Moses, the lawgiver, was about to be put to death by God for breaking the law. God took the sign of the covenant seriously, and Moses should have as well. Moses knew that circumcision was required by law, yet for whatever reason, he had delayed in acting. Finally, his wife Zipporah stepped in to do what Moses had failed to accomplish, thus saving Moses' life. The covenant sign of circumcision that began with Abraham continued to Jacob, Isaac, and the Israelites of the Exodus. They too were the children of Abraham and recipients of the Abrahamic Covenant.13 This ongoing command of circumcision can be seen as we look to the Levitical laws that were later put in place by Moses for the nation of Israel in the book of Leviticus: "And on the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin shall be circumcised."14 This was not a new command but was a reiteration of what God told Abraham, “And Abraham circumcised his son Isaac when he was eight days old, as God had commanded him.”15 The generations that followed Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Moses continued to obey this command of God. As the New Testament opens, we see that even Jesus Christ was circumcised on the eighth day, thus fulfilling the sign of the Abrahamic Covenant. “And at the end of eight days, when he was circumcised, he was called Jesus, the name given by the angel before he was conceived in the womb.”16 It is safe to assume that the apostles, also descendants of Abraham, had been circumcised as well. The Apostle Paul certainly mentions that he was, “If anyone else thinks he has reason for confidence in the flesh, I have more: circumcised on the eighth day of the people of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews ...”17 So, what does this mean for us today? Does God still require circumcision for modern believers? What are we to make of these dire warnings connected to those who withheld this sign? According to the Abrahamic Covenant, does a parent still deserve death if their son is not circumcised on the eighth day?

ALL BELIEVERS ARE CIRCUMCISED

Well, the good news is, if you are a Christian, then you are in the New Covenant that Christ has made on your behalf. The sign of circumcision is no longer required, and God even rejects those who try to maintain this practice as a sign of God’s blessing upon them. Why? Because the covenant sign has been fulfilled in the New Covenant by the Person and work of Jesus Christ. Take the following passages, for example.

But some men came down from Judea and were teaching the brothers, "Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved." And after Paul and Barnabas had no small dissension and debate with them, Paul and Barnabas and some of the others were appointed to go up to Jerusalem to the apostles and the elders about this question. So, being sent on their way by the church, they passed through both Phoenicia and Samaria, describing in detail the conversion of the Gentiles, and brought great joy to all the brothers. When they came to Jerusalem, they were welcomed by the church and the apostles and the elders, and they declared all that God had done with them. But some believers who belonged to the party of the Pharisees rose up and said, "It is necessary to circumcise them and to order them to keep the Law of Moses." The apostles and the elders were gathered together to consider this matter. And after there had been much debate, Peter stood up and said to them, "Brothers, you know that in the early days God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe. And God, who knows the heart, bore witness to them, by giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us, and he made no distinction between us and them, having cleansed their hearts by faith. Now, therefore, why are you putting God to the test by placing a yoke on the neck of the disciples that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? But we believe that we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will. (Acts 15:1-11)

This information was shocking to the Jews who were still holding onto Old Covenant regulations in the New Covenant era. Under the Abrahamic Covenant, those who did not bear the covenant sign of circumcision could not be in the covenant community. However, Peter has seen that God is now saving circumcised and uncircumcised people. The Abrahamic sign of the covenant is no longer required to be in the covenant community. Peter even lets the council know that the uncircumcised Gentiles were saved in the same way that they (the circumcised Jews) were. He makes this point by letting them know that the uncircumcised Gentiles had been given the Holy Spirit upon hearing and believing the gospel.

CIRCUMCISION WAS REPLACED BY SOMETHING GREATER

The Bible is abundantly clear about the cessation of the sign of circumcision. There are numerous passages that speak directly to the issue. For example:

Look: I, Paul, say to you that if you accept circumcision, Christ will be of no advantage to you. I testify again to every man who accepts circumcision that he is obligated to keep the whole law. You are severed from Christ, you who would be justified by the law; you have fallen away from grace. For through the Spirit, by faith, we ourselves eagerly wait for the hope of righteousness. For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything, but only faith working through love. (Galatians 5:2-6) See with what large letters I am writing to you with my own hand. It is those who want to make a good showing in the flesh who would force you to be circumcised, and only in order that they may not be persecuted for the cross of Christ. For even those who are circumcised do not themselves keep the law, but they desire to have you circumcised that they may boast in your flesh. But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world. For neither circumcision counts for anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation. And as for all who walk by this rule, peace and mercy be upon them, and upon the Israel of God. (Galatians 6:11-16) In him also you were circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, by putting off the body of the flesh, by the circumcision of Christ. (Colossians 2:11) Look out for the dogs, look out for the evildoers, look out for those who mutilate the flesh. For we are the circumcision, who worship by the Spirit of God and glory in Christ Jesus and put no confidence in the flesh. (Philippians 3:2-3)

These passages make it abundantly clear that the sign of the Abrahamic Covenant was no longer applicable to the Jews or the Gentiles. Paul argues that there is now no longer any profit to being circumcised. Far from being necessary, it was now considered useless. Paul even calls the Jews who were commanding the Gentiles to be circumcised “dogs,” a term that the Jews often used of the Gentiles who were outside of the faith. Now, those who are outside of the faith are those who are requiring circumcision. Paul also calls them “evildoers,” and “mutilators of the flesh.” How could Paul say such a thing about those who were simply following the commandment of God? Was Paul violating the Abrahamic Covenant by ordering people to abstain from circumcision? Should he have been put to death, as almost happened to Moses? Most Christians will surely say, "No," but there might be a loss of words if asked to explain their answer. So, let’s look to God’s word for the answer to why Paul’s stance on circumcision had changed. Paul writes,

Was anyone at the time of his call already circumcised? Let him not seek to remove the marks of circumcision. Was anyone at the time of his call uncircumcised? Let him not seek circumcision. For neither circumcision counts for anything nor uncircumcision but keeping the commandments of God. (1 Corinthians 7:18-19)

Circumcision doesn’t count for anything. How could Paul say such a thing? Wasn’t circumcision a commandment of God and a requirement to be included among the people of God? So, what happened that Paul could say that circumcision is no longer a commandment? The Messiah had come and had made a better covenant on behalf of His people, thus making the Old Covenant signs no longer a requirement.18 In the New Covenant, all of God’s people are still circumcised, not physically, but spiritually by God Himself. As Paul teaches, the physical circumcision of the past finds its typological fulfillment in the circumcision that the Holy Spirit accomplishes.

For no one is a Jew who is merely one outwardly, nor is circumcision outward and physical. But a Jew is one inwardly, and circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the letter. (Romans 2:28-29)

The outward physical sign of the Abrahamic Covenant had been replaced by a greater circumcision, the circumcision of the heart. This circumcision is done supernaturally by God to all who are saved. This can also be seen in Paul’s writing to the Colossians:

In him also you were circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, by putting off the body of the flesh, by the circumcision of Christ. (Colossians 2:11)

As part of the New Covenant Christ fulfilled, all believers, by the work of the Holy Spirit, have received a spiritual circumcision, the circumcision of Christ.

NEW COVENANT CIRCUMCISION

Now that we have established that there is no need for physical circumcision and that it is now inward, not outward, let’s explore the New Covenant circumcision. If we go back to the writings of Moses, we can see that the sign of the Old Abrahamic Covenant was a physical act that pointed to a greater spiritual lesson. In this sense, circumcision was revelatory as it pointed forward to the need for an inward heart circumcision.

Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no longer stubborn. (Deuteronomy 10:16) And the LORD your God will circumcise your heart and the heart of your offspring, so that you will love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul, that you may live. (Deuteronomy 30:6)

The ultimate issue is that the people needed a heart that loved God and put away sin. God would do this for all who were obedient. The problem was that none were. The people of Israel continually rebelled against God and broke the covenant. However, there was one Israelite who obeyed God perfectly: Jesus Christ. He is the One with a heart that has been perfectly circumcised and loves God with all his heart and soul. We who believe in Him, reap the benefits of His obedience. Through the Person and work of Jesus Christ, God circumcises the hearts of all who are in His household. This new heart which God gives through the New Covenant is elaborated on greatly in Jeremiah:19

Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah, not like the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt, my covenant that they broke, though I was their husband, declares the LORD. For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, declares the LORD: I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts. And I will be their God, and they shall be my people. (Jeremiah 31:31-33)

As Jeremiah writes about the rebellious hearts of the Israelites who have broken God’s covenant, he announces that there will be a day when God will make a New Covenant and that He will accomplish what the Old Covenant could not do, circumcision of the heart. This operation is done not by man, but by God Himself for all who are in the New Covenant. Paul elaborates on this greatly as he is living in the New Covenant and writing to the people of the New Covenant.

There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus. And if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise. (Galatians 3:28-29) For through the Spirit, by faith, we ourselves eagerly wait for the hope of righteousness. For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything, but only faith working through love. (Galatians 5:5-6)

Abraham’s offspring were to receive the future promises, signified by circumcision. Paul states that both Jews (people physically related to Abraham), and Greeks (all people and nations not physically related to Abraham) are heirs to the promises that Abraham received by grace through faith in Jesus Christ. The physical separation of skin commanded under the Abrahamic Covenant had now found its spiritual fulfillment in what Christ had accomplished for the believer.

WATER BAPTISM DID NOT REPLACE CIRCUMCISION

Many who prescribe to Covenant Theology believe that the sign of the Abrahamic Covenant, circumcision, was replaced by water baptism; however, the sign of the Mosaic Covenant, the Sabbath, has remained the same. This is an inconsistent interpretation of the fulfillment of covenant signs. If baptism replaced circumcision, we would certainly expect God to have declared this in His word, especially in the passages that teach there is no longer any need for circumcision. However, such a replacement is found nowhere in Scripture. If something so serious as circumcision, which required the death penalty if not observed, had been replaced with baptism, then we would expect to find this taught by Christ and the Apostles throughout the New Testament. But we don't; instead, we find circumcision of the Old Covenant replaced, not with another sign, but with the work of Christ in salvation for His covenant people. Sadly, many people who adhere to Covenant Theology believe that infant baptism must be administered to young babies and children to place them in the New Covenant.20 However, this is a confusion of covenants and a practice with no biblical warrant. Such a person does not see the distinctions between the Old and New Covenants. We are not to replace Old Covenant signs with new ones. Instead, we are to see the old covenants and their signs as obsolete. As the author of Hebrews says, "In speaking of a new covenant, he makes the first one obsolete. And what is becoming obsolete and growing old is ready to vanish away."21 Paul has made it clear that there is no need for the physical act of circumcision, and there is certainly no need to create a physical replacement for it, especially when it is not warranted by Scripture. Within the New Covenant, unlike the Old Covenant, we find that the covenant is made up of 100% believers.22 This is why we do not have record of a single infant being baptized in the New Testament. Adherents to Covenant Theology who baptize their unbelieving babies and children do not understand this difference and attempt to do what man cannot accomplish.23 Instead of relying on the Holy Spirit to truly place a person into the New Covenant by giving the person faith to believe in the gospel for salvation, and then being baptized as a sign of salvation, they place unbelievers into the New Covenant community themselves by water baptism. God never gave a command to baptize babies or children prior to salvation; nor do we have any Biblical record of a person who has not believed in Christ for their salvation being baptized. Instead, we see that people were only baptized after they believed in the gospel for salvation.24 Summary: So, to return to our original question, "What does the Sabbath have to do with circumcision?" Both are signs of previous covenants, were required by the command of God, and came with severe repercussions if not obeyed. However, now that the New Covenant has come, neither the physical sign of circumcision nor the Sabbath day rest are required. The Abrahamic Covenant and the Mosaic Covenant, and the signs that accompanied them, were typological and found their fulfillment in the New Covenant made by Jesus Christ for all His covenant people.

11 Genesis 17:9-11

12 Exodus 31:13-17

14 Leviticus 12:3

20 Guy Richard, “Paedobaptism,” Tabletalk, April 1, 2020, https://tabletalkmagazine.com/article/2020/04/paedobaptism/.
