sections.title: CHAPTER 6: WHY DID GOD COMMAND THE SABBATH TO BE OBSERVED?
sections.html:
To understand God's command to keep the Sabbath days, one must understand why God gave it in the first place. As we look to Scripture for our answer, we find that the Sabbath command was given to Israel for two reasons, the first given in Exodus 20 and the second given in Deuteronomy 5. Both reasons are part of what is commonly known as the Ten Commandments. We will start with Deuteronomy 5 first since it is often neglected, and we will later circle back to the reason for the Sabbath given in Exodus 20. Deuteronomy 5 gives the Commandments in short and concise orders like: "You shall not murder." "You shall not commit adultery." "You shall not steal." and "You shall not bear false witness against

th

your neighbor." However, the 4 Commandment to “Observe the Sabbath day,” comes with an explanation. God not only commands it, but He gives the reason (the why) for its establishment.25 The other commands needed no or little explanation because the activity which each one forbade was commonly known to be sinful. However, observing the Sabbath was not normative to humanity, Moses, or the

th

Israelites. The 4 Commandment needed further explanation because it was a new command connected to the recent freedom from slavery that God had accomplished for Israel. Therefore, God did not just say "Observe the Sabbath" and stop there, as He did with other commandments. Instead, an explanation was given with this command. Otherwise, the Israelites would have had no clue why they were to set this one day apart. Note the commentary that God

th

gave with the 4 Commandment:

Observe the Sabbath day, to keep it holy, as the LORD your God commanded you. Six days you shall labor and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God. On it you shall not do any work, you or your son or your daughter or your male servant or your female servant, or your ox or your donkey or any of your livestock, or the sojourner who is within your gates, that your male servant and your female servant may rest as well as you. You shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God brought you out from there with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm. Therefore, the LORD your God commanded you to keep the Sabbath day. (Deuteronomy 5:12-15)

In verse fifteen, we find the exact reason God commanded the Israelites to keep the Sabbath. They were to use the day to remember that God had freed them from slavery. God had redeemed the Israelites from slavery, and the Sabbath was to become the weekly reminder of God's magnificent work on their behalf. Israel had no weapons, no military, no ability to fight the Egyptians, and no chance to escape. However, God had supernaturally delivered them from the most powerful nation on earth. Every seventh day, the entire nation was to stop working and remember that by God’s "mighty hand and an outstretched arm," they had been set free. Another passage that gives additional clarity on the reason why the Israelites were commanded to observe the Sabbath day is found in Ezekiel.

Moreover, I gave them my Sabbaths, as a sign between me and them, that they might know that I am the LORD who sanctifies them. But the house of Israel rebelled against me in the wilderness. They did not walk in my statutes but rejected my rules, by which, if a person does them, he shall live; and my Sabbaths they greatly profaned." Then I said I would pour out my wrath upon them in the wilderness, to make a full end of them. But I acted for the sake of my name, that it should not be profaned in the sight of the nations, in whose sight I had brought them out. (Ezekiel 20:12-14)

In this passage, God explicitly states who He gave the Sabbaths to and why. From this passage, we can see that Israel was the only nation that God commanded to obey the Sabbath. God gave them the Sabbath to be a sign of the covenant that God made with Israel. In verse twelve, God says that the Sabbaths were given to Israel "that they might know that I am the Lord who sanctifies them." The word “sanctify” has to do with something or someone being set apart for holy use. As we look back at God's calling Israel out from slavery, that is precisely what He did. He separated Israel from all other nations to be separated unto Him. The sign of them being separated for holy use by God was to be the Sabbaths. No other nation was commanded to keep the Sabbaths because God had only made this covenant with Israel. The act of God separating Israel for holy use can be seen in many places, but Deuteronomy 7 is certainly a notable example:

For you are a people holy to the LORD your God. The LORD your God has chosen you to be a people for his treasured possession, out of all the peoples who are on the face of the earth. It was not because you were more in number than any other people that the LORD set his love on you and chose you, for you were the fewest of all peoples, but it is because the LORD loves you and is keeping the oath that he swore to your fathers, that the LORD has brought you out with a mighty hand and redeemed you from the house of slavery, from the hand of Pharaoh king of Egypt. Know therefore that the LORD your God is God, the faithful God who keeps covenant and steadfast love with those who love him and keep his commandments, to a thousand generations, and repays to their face those who hate him, by destroying them. He will not be slack with one who hates him. He will repay him to his face. You shall therefore be careful to do the commandment and the statutes and the rules that I command you today. (Deuteronomy 7:6-11)

From this passage, we see sanctification language being used in a similar way as was found in Ezekiel 20. God had "chosen" Israel "out of all the peoples who are on the face of the earth" to be "holy to the Lord your God." The Israelites had been set apart (sanctified) for God. Israel had been set apart, made holy by God, and with that, God set apart one day from the rest of the week to also be holy. The holy day was to be a weekly reminder to the Israelites that they were a holy people. God had not covenanted with any other nation; therefore, no other nation was commanded to have a holy day to reflect on such a covenant.

You shall keep the Sabbath, because it is holy for you. Everyone who profanes it shall be put to death. Whoever does any work on it, that soul shall be cut off from among his people. Six days shall work be done, but the seventh day is a Sabbath of solemn rest, holy to the LORD. Whoever does any work on the Sabbath day shall be put to death. Therefore the people of Israel shall keep the Sabbath, observing the Sabbath throughout their generations, as a covenant forever. It is a sign forever between me and the people of Israel that in six days the LORD made heaven and earth, and on the seventh day he rested and was refreshed. (Exodus 31:14-17)

From the passage, it can be seen that the Israelites were commanded to keep the day holy. It was to be set apart from common use and was to be a day of rest. This was due to the fact that God had made covenant with them. According to verses 16-17, the Sabbath was a sign of that covenant. Sadly, Covenant Theologians often use this passage to attempt to prove that keeping the Sabbath day has been a command of God since creation because the work and rest of God is mentioned. In fact, in Exodus 20, this is another reason for keeping the Sabbath. But as we discovered in a previous chapter, the claim of Covenant Theology that God was reiterating what had always been true, that the Sabbath day was always set apart and holy for humanity, is not correct. If we let Scripture speak for itself, it is impossible to come to such a conclusion, especially in light of the entire teaching of Scripture. For instance, read back over the above passage or read Exodus 20. Does it say anything about the Sabbath day being a command since the creation of the world? No. Does it say that keeping the Sabbath was a command given to all mankind? No. Instead, God commands only Israel to follow the same pattern of work and rest that He did at creation. Even if we look back at the Genesis account from which this passage draws, we still do not find such reasoning for the Sabbath.

Thus the heavens and the earth were finished, and all the host of them. And on the seventh day, God finished his work that he had done, and he rested on the seventh day from all his work that he had done. So God blessed the seventh day and made it holy, because on it God rested from all his work that he had done in creation. (Genesis 2:1-3)

If we read the passage and do not allow preconceived theological tainting to enter our reading, it is simple to see that God gave no command to Adam and Eve, nor the rest of mankind, to keeping the seventh day free from work. No matter how many times one reads over this passage, such a conclusion cannot be derived. Instead, the passage emphasizes that God made everything in six days and then stopped the work of creation. Summary: Why did God command the Sabbath to be observed? It is important to consider when God commanded the Sabbath to be observed and whom God commanded to observe it. Then and only then can one really begin to see the reason behind such a command. As we have seen, there is no mention of anyone ever keeping or breaking the Sabbath command in the book of Genesis because God had not given it. It was not until God made a covenant with Israel that He commanded the Sabbath to be observed. God had chosen Israel and set them apart for His holy use. Likewise, He commanded them to set apart the seventh day as a type of visual aid, a sign, of the covenant that God had made with them. With these passages in mind, are Christians required to keep the seventh-day Sabbath? Again, we must let Scripture speak for itself and not add or subtract from it. God explicitly gave the Sabbath day to the nation of Israel as the sign of the Mosaic Covenant. Christians are not national Israel, nor have we been set free from slavery from Egypt. We are also not under the Mosaic Covenant. That covenant was for a specific people for a specific time, and that goes for the sign of the covenant as well. We will continue to explore what this means to modern Christians in the coming chapters.

25 Deuteronomy 5:17-20

sections.title: CHAPTER 7: WHAT DOES PAUL SAY ABOUT THE SABBATH?
sections.html:
Under the Old Covenant, the consequences of violating the Sabbath were severe. Working on the Sabbath even resulted in the death penalty. Not observing the seven-year Sabbath led to Israel receiving the wrath of God, resulting in slaughter, slavery, and being removed from the land of promise by their enemy. So, where does that leave us now? Would you deserve the death penalty if you worked on Sunday? Does our nation, like Israel, deserve the wrath of God since we have not honored the seven-year Sabbaths? Let's begin by examining what the Apostle Paul says about the Sabbath. Paul, a Pharisee of Pharisees, was raised in the Old Covenant, was taught by the who’s who of the teachers of the law and became a great defender of the Old Covenant law.26 However, when Paul became a Christian, he realized that God gave the entire Old Covenant for many reasons but first and foremost, to lead us to Christ. In Christ, Paul came to see that the Old Covenant was now fulfilled in the ratification of a New Covenant. So how will the great defender of the laws of the Old Covenant deal with the sign of that covenant now that a New Covenant has come? Will Paul command Christians to maintain the Sabbath regulations as the Israelites did under the Old Covenant? Will he lessen the Sabbath regulations? Or will he completely dismiss the Old Covenant Sabbath regulations? Let's find out. In all of Paul's writings, the Sabbath is barely even mentioned. From the rarity of Sabbath teaching alone, we see that something has certainly changed from its primary place of importance under the Old Covenant. When we read the writings of Paul, violation of the seventh day was no longer punishable by death, and observation of the Sabbath day was no longer required. Paul did not recommend that the Sabbath day be treated differently from the rest. Such conclusions can be easily proven by openly and honestly looking at Paul’s own words.

GALATIANS AND THE SABBATH

But now that you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God, how can you turn back again to the weak and worthless elementary principles of the world, whose slaves you want to be once more? You observe days and months and seasons and years! I am afraid I may have labored over you in vain. (Galatians 4:9-11)

In Galatia, the Judaizers pressured the Gentile Christians to become Jewish and do things according to the Old Covenant. The Judaizers were not giving the proper emphasis to Christ and His work for salvation. Instead, they were returning to imposing regulations of the Old Covenant, including Sabbath regulations and even circumcision. Those who were making circumcision a requirement were dangerously adding to the gospel of Christ. Paul said, "Look: I, Paul, say to you that if you accept circumcision, Christ will be of no advantage to you."27 This covenantal requirement was now "no advantage" to those in the New Covenant. Why did it lose its importance? Paul could say this because the sign and shadow of circumcision had been fulfilled in the salvation that Christ had accomplished for His people. In the same vein, the Judaizers were pressuring the Galatian Christians to keep the Jewish holy days, including Sabbath days. How does Paul handle the situation? He does not put up with it and manages it much like he argues about circumcision. Paul views any such pressure to keep Sabbath day regulations as wrong. Under the New Covenant, the Sabbath regulations were no longer required. Those bent on believing that the Old Covenant Sabbath regulations were still required caused Paul much concern over their salvation. So much so that he "fears that he may have labored in vain." Paul had already given them the gospel of Jesus Christ, and that was sufficient for salvation.28 He did not command them to observe the Sabbaths and special days of the Old Covenant. Why? Because the theological lessons that those special days, months, seasons, and years pointed to had now come to fruition in the coming of the One who would provide ultimate rest for their souls, the Messiah. Paul, a pharisee of Pharisees, a man trained by the best teacher of the law in his day, Gamaliel, now saw that the days of required Sabbath-keeping were given under the Old Covenant and were no longer required under the New Covenant. And anyone who was returning to such days caused Paul to question whether they were truly saved. Jesus Christ had announced a drastic change. No longer were people required under penalty of death to remember that God had redeemed them from Egypt. Now they had been redeemed from the bondage of sin by the Son of God Himself. The emphasis was now on the accomplished work of Jesus Christ, not the previous work of God in bringing Israel out of Egypt. The Jews were trying to make something that had been important, the Exodus, more important than what the Exodus pointed to, the salvation of God's people by the Messiah. Therefore, such an emphasis on the observation of special days made Paul question the people's salvation. Instead of resting in Christ, they were going back to resting on certain days. The Jews were making the Old Covenant more important than the New Covenant and making days more important than their fulfillment through the work of Christ.

COLOSSIANS AND THE SABBATH

In Paul's letter to the Colossians, we find that he must deal with some of the same problems faced by those who were emphasizing the Old Covenant regulations instead of seeing their fulfillment in Jesus Christ. If there was any question of Paul's view of the Sabbath, it is made clear in his letter to the Colossians. He writes, Therefore let no one pass judgment on you in questions of food and drink, or about a festival or a new moon or a Sabbath. These are a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ. (Colossians 2:16-17) To rightly understand this passage, we must understand what Paul means by "shadows," and "substance." For starters, what is a shadow? They are theological lessons that find their fullest meaning in something greater than themselves. This we can see as Paul list four Old Covenant shadows that have now found the substance of their fulfillment in Jesus Christ. Like what we found in Galatians, the Colossian believers were being judged for not keeping the required regulations under the Old Covenant that God made with the Israelites. Why does Paul tell them not to judge people who "break" these Old Covenant laws? Because under the Old Covenant, God commanded them to pass judgment on one another for these things. However, the theological purpose for those shadows had now come in the Person and work of Jesus Christ. They were not to go back to the shadows but instead to look at the actual Person of whom the shadows were pointing. To understand the shadows that Paul is referring to, let's consider each of the categories that Paul mentions:

1. "Therefore let no one pass judgment on you in questions of food and drink."

The first thing that Paul says that no one is to pass judgment on is "food and drink." Under the Old Covenant, God gave Israel strict dietary laws, which helped to separate them from the other nations. These were far more than dietary suggestions from God; these were commands, and to violate them was a sin against God.

This is the law about beast and bird and every living creature that moves through the waters and every creature that swarms on the ground, to make a distinction between the unclean and the clean and between the living creature that may be eaten and the living creature that may not be eaten. (Leviticus 11:46- 47)

Under the Old Covenant, there were stringent dietary rules the Israelites were required to obey. So, what about today? Are the dietary laws of the Old Covenant required for Christians under the New Covenant? No. However, it took a lot of convincing to get the early Jewish Christians to understand that the dietary laws had been lifted. Even with divine intervention, the Apostle Peter still had to be told multiple times. In Acts 10, years after Jesus had risen from the dead and ascended into heaven, Peter was still adhering to the Old Covenant dietary regulations. At this point in history, the gospel of salvation had come to the Jews, [29] Samaritans,30 and now God wanted the gospel to go to Gentiles. However, there was a big obstacle, the Gentiles were considered unclean, and the food they ate was considered unclean. These dietary differences made it impossible for Peter ever to enjoy the hospitality of a Gentile invitation to dinner to discuss the saving message of Jesus Christ. But all of that was about to change. God spoke to Peter through a vision in which Peter, while very hungry, saw a large sheet containing both clean and unclean animals and was commanded by God to eat them.

In it were all kinds of animals and reptiles and birds of the air. And there came a voice to him: "Rise, Peter; kill and eat." But Peter said, "By no means, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean." And the voice came to him again a second time, "What God has made clean, do not call common." This happened three times, and the thing was taken up at once to heaven. (Acts 10:12-16)

Peter was horrified at the possibility of disobeying the dietary laws that God Himself had put into place with the Old Covenant. Remember, these rules had been in place for the Jewish people for over a thousand years. He had abided by these rules all his life, and the Jewish culture was still abiding by. Not only was it their tradition and custom, but as Peter voiced, they still believed that it was a sin to break the Old Covenant dietary laws.31 This vision and message from the Lord are not just about teaching Peter that he is now allowed to eat bacon (even though that is a critical point to remember). The main point is that God had lifted the dietary restrictions that separated the Jews from the Gentiles. The Old Covenant restrictions about unclean food and fellowshipping with unclean people, the Gentiles, had been removed. Peter follows through with the message of the vision, goes to the home of an unclean Gentile Centurion, eats unclean food, shares the gospel with unclean people, and the unclean Gentiles are made clean. This news traveled quickly, but like all gossip, some parts gained more traction than others. The main news story of the day was that the Apostle Peter went into the home of a Gentile and ate Gentile food. This becomes evident as we look at Acts 15, when Peter is called to account for his fellowship with Gentiles.

Now the apostles and the brothers who were throughout Judea heard that the Gentiles also had received the word of God. So when Peter went up to Jerusalem, the circumcision party criticized him, saying, "You went to uncircumcised men and ate with them." (Acts 11:1-3)

Notice that the primary influencers of this questioning are the "circumcision party." According to Paul, these were professing Christians who still believed that there was value in receiving the Old Covenant sign of circumcision even though it was now worthless. The same group clinging to the Old Covenant sign is also clinging to the Old Covenant dietary guidelines. They cannot understand how a Jew, even a Christian Jew, much less the chief Apostle, could violate the Old Covenant dietary laws. For this behavior, they demand an answer from Peter, and an answer they receive:

But Peter began and explained it to them in order: "I was in the city of Joppa praying, and in a trance I saw a vision, something like a great sheet descending, being let down from heaven by its four corners, and it came down to me. Looking at it closely, I observed animals and beasts of prey and reptiles and birds of the air. And I heard a voice saying to me, 'Rise, Peter; kill and eat.' But I said, 'By no means, Lord; for nothing common or unclean has ever entered my mouth.' But the voice answered a second time from heaven, 'What God has made clean, do not call common.' this happened three times, and all was drawn up again into heaven. And behold, at that very moment three men arrived at the house in which we were, sent to me from Caesarea. And the Spirit told me to go with them, making no distinction. These six brothers also accompanied me, and we entered the man's house. And he told us how he had seen the angel stand in his house and say, 'Send to Joppa and bring Simon who is called Peter; he will declare to you a message by which you will be saved, you and all your household.' As I began to speak, the Holy Spirit fell on them just as on us at the beginning. And I remembered the word of the Lord, how he said, 'John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.' If then God gave the same gift to them as he gave to us when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I that I could stand in God's way?" When they heard these things they fell silent. And they glorified God, saying, "Then to the Gentiles also God has granted repentance that leads to life." (Acts 11:4- 18)

I do not feel that much explanation is needed for Peter's answer. However, I want you to see the connection between Peter eating with the Gentiles, being saved, and receiving the Holy Spirit. The Jerusalem council "fell silent" as they processed all that this meant. God had removed the Old Covenant food restrictions, and on top of that, the Old Covenant sign of circumcision now meant nothing. Under the New Covenant, the people of God were made up of both Jews and Gentiles! What does all of this have to do with Paul’s writing to the Colossians? The same theological point that God made with Peter, and Peter made to the Jerusalem Council, is being made by Paul to the Colossians. According to the New Covenant, they should not judge anyone according to the Old Covenant dietary laws because such restrictions, as Peter had found out, were not a part of the New Covenant.

2. "Therefore let no one pass judgment on you in questions of … a festival."

What's wrong with a festival? Again, this passage would not make much sense without understanding what a festival was under the Old Covenant. One might even assume that we are not to gather with people to eat. But obviously, this is not what Paul is talking about, for the specific festivals Paul mentions are far more than just a party. These festivals were mandatory under the Old Covenant, were packed with meaning, and served as theological "shadows" that found their full meaning, or "substance," in Christ. To get a basic understanding of these festivals, we must return to the commands connected to the Old Covenant that were given to Israel at Mt. Sinai.

"Three times in the year you shall keep a feast to me. You shall keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread. As I commanded you, you shall eat unleavened bread for seven days at the appointed time in the month of Abib, for in it you came out of Egypt. None shall appear before me empty-handed. You shall keep the Feast of Harvest, of the first fruits of your labor, of what you sow in the field. You shall keep the Feast of Ingathering at the end of the year, when you gather in from the field the fruit of your labor. Three times in the year shall all your males appear before the Lord God." (Exodus 23:14-17) Three times a year all your men must appear before the Lord your God at the place he will choose: at the Festival of Unleavened Bread, the Festival of Weeks and the Festival of Tabernacles. (Deuteronomy 16:16)

As you can see, these feasts, or festivals, were not optional but mandatory requirements for the Israelites. God put these feasts in place to teach the people valuable theological truths that Christ would ultimately fulfill. Take the first feast, for example, The Passover. This was a festival that God instituted since the Exodus of the Israelites from Egypt. However, on the night of Jesus' betrayal, He takes the Passover meal with His disciples as usual but then makes a monumental announcement that would forever change the Passover.

Now as they were eating, Jesus took bread, and after blessing it broke it and gave it to the disciples, and said, "Take, eat; this is my body." And he took a cup, and when he had given thanks he gave it to them, saying, "Drink of it, all of you, for this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins. (Matthew 26:26-28)

Jesus explained to His disciples that He was the literal embodiment of the Passover. As with the spotless lamb sacrificed at the time of the original Passover in Exodus, Jesus was the sinless Lamb of God that had come to provide forgiveness of sins. This forgiveness meant that all who He represents would not suffer the wrath of God that our sin deserves, but instead, the wrath would pass over us and onto the One who took the punishment in our place. Upon Jesus' death, there was no longer any need for Christians to participate in that feast or the others because they were shadows that pointed to something greater that was to come. Now, we take of the Lord's Supper, which points to the sufficiency of Christ's sacrifice to take away our sin, provide forgiveness, and reminds us that we will eat and drink with our Savior again one day. Long story short, are you now required by God to celebrate the Old Covenant festivals? No. Why not? Because God used them to teach about the Messiah that was to come and has now come. Instead of looking back at the shadows, we now look to the substance of Christ.

3. "Therefore let no one pass judgment on you in questions of … a New Moon."

Have you judged anyone regarding a New Moon lately? Most likely not. Most Christians have no idea what Paul is even talking about concerning not passing judgment on people celebrating a New Moon. So, what does he mean by this prohibition? As with the other components in this list of Paul's, we find that this was an activity that God specifically commanded to Israel under the Old Covenant. God commanded Israel to have a sacrifice at the beginning of each month, coinciding with the phase of the moon known as the "new moon.” This sacrifice became known as the New Moon sacrifice. The Hebrew word for "month" (Hodesh) means "new moon." This specific sacrifice is laid out for us to read about in the book of Numbers.

At the beginnings of your months, you shall offer a burnt offering to the LORD: two bulls from the herd, one ram, seven male lambs a year old without blemish; also three tenths of an ephah of fine flour for a grain offering, mixed with oil, for each bull, and two tenths of fine flour for a grain offering, mixed with oil, for the one ram; and a tenth of fine flour mixed with oil as a grain offering for every lamb; for a burnt offering with a pleasing aroma, a food offering to the LORD. Their drink offerings shall be half a hin of wine for a bull, a third of a hin for a ram, and a quarter of a hin for a lamb. This is the burnt offering of each month throughout the months of the year. Also one male goat for a sin offering to the LORD; it shall be offered besides the regular burnt offering and its drink offering. (Numbers 28:11-15)

So, what were believers to do under the New Covenant? Did God still require the New Moon Sacrifices? Or what about us today? Should we still gather the bulls, sheep, goats, flour, etc., at the beginning of each month for a sacrifice? I believe most Christians would agree that the answer to such questions is, "No." But there might be some confusion if asked to explain why the answer is, "No." The answer is because Jesus Christ was the supreme sacrifice that fully accomplished what all other sacrifices for sin could only foreshadow. Consider the words of the voice of the one God sent to announce the Messiah, John the Baptist: "The next day he saw Jesus coming toward him, and said, "Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!"32 God had provided the final and ultimate sacrifice of which all other sacrifices pointed. As with all other sacrifices, the New Moon sacrifices were shadows/types of the substance, which is Jesus Christ. Paul let the Colossian believers know that they should not judge anyone if they were no longer participating in the New Moon sacrifice at the temple. The New Moon sacrifices had served their purpose but were now no longer required by the people of God.

4. "Therefore let no one pass judgment on you in questions of… Sabbath."

Finally, we get to the main point that we are analyzing in this passage, Paul's teaching about the Sabbath. It is imperative not to isolate the mention of "Sabbath" in this passage but see that Paul places "Sabbath" in a list of Old Covenant regulations that were strictly part of the Old Covenant and were no longer required by the people of God under the New Covenant. All four of these prohibitions of judgment are in the same category: shadows, which are no longer needed because the substance had now come. Interestingly, some Christians will read over this passage and quickly grasp the shadow and substance point that Paul is making regarding the Old Covenant diets, feasts, and sacrifices. However, when it comes to the next word in his list of Old Covenant laws, "Sabbath," they skip right over it as if it were not in the same category as the other three that he had just mentioned. But this vital point must not be skipped. Now that the New Covenant had arrived, the believers could not be judged by the Sabbath regulations of the Old Covenant. This prohibition from Sabbath judgment was a highly significant change in the culture and tradition of the Jews who had become Christians. To understand just how big of a deal this is, we must recall how under the Old Covenant, if any Israelite dishonored the Sabbath, he was to be judged and stoned to death.33 How does that compare to Paul's teaching on the Sabbath now that the New Covenant had come? Paul says, "no one" can be judged about what they do or do not do on the Sabbath. This truth was for Christians who were Jew or Gentile. The Sabbath was now just another day that they could live as they did on the other six days of the week. Has this key point been applied to Christianity as much as the other three in Paul's list? What if you saw someone mowing his yard on a day, be that Saturday (the Old Covenant Sabbath) or Sunday (the Lord's Day)? Is he in sin? Should you judge them? Should you confront such a person and encourage him to confess and repent of breaking the Sabbath? What if he will not stop mowing his yard, even after he is confronted, and even makes a habit of doing yard work on the day that you consider the Sabbath? Do you then proceed further and bring other believers to confront him? Do you bring him before the church for excommunication if he will not stop? Hmm. Let's ask Paul, "Therefore let no one pass judgment on you in questions of… Sabbath." Sadly, many Christians, churches, and adherents to Covenantal Theology will not allow Scripture to be authoritative on this issue. On another note, but a similar one, it is also worth noting that Paul makes no mention of the Old Covenant Sabbath day, which was Saturday, being changed to another day, such as Sunday. This would have been the perfect place for Paul to teach that a crucial transition of Sabbath days had happened under the covenantal change from Old to New. However, nothing is mentioned of such a change in days. Even though Christ rose from the dead on a Sunday, and we find early Christians worshiping corporately on Sundays, Paul does not impose the Old Covenant Sabbath sign or regulations upon it. He makes no mention of a new day being the fulfillment of the Old Covenant shadow. Instead, what does he point to as the fulfillment of the Sabbath? Jesus Christ. The substance of which the Old Covenant Sabbath shadow was pointing was not towards another day but towards the Person and work of Jesus Christ, who completed all things regarding salvation on our behalf. As we wrap up Paul's New Covenant teaching regarding the Old Covenant shadows, it is certainly worth comparing Paul's words to the Colossians under the New Covenant to God's word to Israel during the Old Covenant.

Therefore let no one pass judgment on you in questions of food and drink, or with regard to a festival or a new moon or a Sabbath. These are a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ. (Colossians 2:16-17) Behold, I am about to build a house for the name of the LORD my God and dedicate it to him for the burning of incense of sweet spices before him, and for the regular arrangement of the showbread, and for burnt offerings morning and evening, on the Sabbaths and the new moons and the appointed feasts of the LORD our God, as ordained forever for Israel. (2 Chronicles 2:4)

These passages represent God's instructions to two different audiences under two different covenants. The Israelites under the Old Covenant were to abide by these instructions strictly. As we have seen, such rules were not mere suggestions by God, but mandatory requirements. However, Paul, writing under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit to the Christians in Colossae, says that there is no longer any need to abide by them because they have found their fulfillment in the Person and work of Jesus Christ.

ROMANS AND THE SABBATH

Paul also addresses whether Christians were to condemn fellow believers who were no longer honoring the Sabbath. Should those no longer honoring the Sabbath day be stoned, removed from the church, treated as non-believers, or what? Many people are shocked to find that the Apostle Paul barely mentions the Sabbath day, and when it is mentioned, the discourse reveals that a major change has

th

happened to the 4 Commandment. Paul does rebuke some Christians regarding Sabbath keeping in this passage, but he does not rebuke those who are not keeping it, but those who are keeping it and forcing others to do the same.

Who are you to pass judgment on the servant of another? It is before his own master that he stands or falls. And he will be upheld, for the Lord is able to make him stand. One person esteems one day as better than another, while another esteems all days alike. Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind. The one who observes the day, observes it in honor of the Lord. The one who eats, eats in honor of the Lord, since he gives thanks to God, while the one who abstains, abstains in honor of the Lord and gives thanks to God. (Romans 14:4-6)

Did Paul view the observation of the Sabbath day holy as a requirement for the Roman Christians? No, if he did, this was the perfect opportunity to state that the Sabbath days instituted by God to Israel must remain, but instead, Paul makes the opposite point. He teaches that every day, including the seventh day, is now equal in importance. Not only were they no longer required by covenantal law to honor the Sabbath, but they were also no longer allowed to judge anyone who chose not to observe the Sabbath. This is a massive change from God telling the Israelites to stone to death the Sabbath-breaker who was picking up sticks.34 Paul teaches the Roman believers that the Old Covenant dietary regulations and Sabbath day observations were now no longer required. These shadows were no longer necessary since the substance, Jesus Christ, had come. Paul had no problem with the Jewish Christians, who were convinced that they should honor certain days and abstain from certain foods, but they were not to make it a requirement or insist that other Christians agree with them. There was freedom to observe these days or not to observe them, as long as they understood that the rest that the Sabbath day typified was realized in Jesus Christ. Summary: The writings of Paul should remove all mystery from whether or not Christians are required to observe the Sabbath. He writes about the Sabbath three separate times, and each time, he removes it as a requirement for Christians. Not only are Christians not required to keep it, but Paul was even concerned about the salvation of the Galatians, who believed that they were required by law to keep the Sabbath still. He wanted believers to see that the time of the Old Covenant had passed, the typologies had been fulfilled, and the substance of our salvation is Christ alone. We must remember that Paul had been a Pharisee, a teacher of the law, “educated at the feet of Gamaliel according to the strict manner of the law.”35 In other words, he was an expert in Old Covenant rules and regulations. He had studied under the best teacher of the law and had become a teacher of the Old Covenant law, but when he was saved, he became a teacher of the law of Christ.36 He was now able to see that what the Sabbath of the Old Covenant symbolized had been fulfilled once and for all in the work of Christ and our rest in Him.

sections.title: CHAPTER 8: WHAT DOES THE AUTHOR OF HEBREWS SAY ABOUT THE SABBATH?
sections.html:
The book of Hebrews operates like a commentary in how it interprets the Old Covenant in light of the New Covenant. It is written to believers who were steeped in the knowledge of the Old Testament and who were also aware of the life, death, resurrection, and ascension of Jesus Christ. The problem was that they lived in a time when the Old Covenant regulations, priests, and sacrifices were still in effect. Even though the Messiah had lived, died, rose, established a New Covenant, and ascended into heaven, most of the Jews had rejected Jesus and continued to live under the Old Covenant rules and regulations. The author of Hebrews has to address the New Covenant believers about how to rightly view the Old Covenant now that the Messiah had come. They were under pressure to return to the Old Covenant, but the author reminds them that the Old Covenant is finished and that the only thing that matters now is the New Covenant that Christ has made. Throughout the book, there is repeated exaltation of the supremacy of Jesus. He is greater than the angels, patriarchs, Moses, Joshua, Aaron, priests, the temple, and all previous sacrifices. The author spends much of his letter comparing and contrasting the Old Covenant to the New Covenant. In this comparison and contrast, the author uses the Sabbath language of the Old Covenant to reveal that a new and greater Sabbath has come. To begin, let's use Hebrews 4 as our focal point:

Therefore, while the promise of entering his rest still stands, let us fear lest any of you should seem to have failed to reach it. (Hebrews 4:1)

What is the "rest" that the author of Hebrews is talking about? Was he encouraging his readers to reenact the literal Israelite exodus from Egypt and subsequent entrance into the land of promise to find rest? Of course not. Is the author encouraging the readers to cease all physical labor on the Sabbath? No. However, he uses the Sabbath language of rest to make a more significant point. The author of Hebrews is using the journey of the Israelites to their promised "rest" as a pattern or type of something greater. Remember, typology is a pattern given by God to point to something, indeed Someone greater. Various persons, events, institutions, and even places, prophetically anticipate the coming of Christ who is the fulfillment or antitype of these typological patterns. This is why types point forward to the Person and work of the Messiah. In the case of the Israelites' entrance into the land, God intended to point to something greater, namely, the rest that would ultimately come in Christ. Let us see how this is so. The words "rest" and "Sabbath" are used in this chapter as a type or pattern that points to the greater eternal rest that believers enter to find permanent rest. This truth becomes increasingly evident as we compare the original rest that was to occur in the Promised Land to the rest that the reader is to enter. Like the Israelites who believed entered the Promised Land to find rest, there is now a greater promised destination and a greater rest that the reader must enter. This "rest" is not a place on earth like Canaan was to the Israelites, but to something better. This point is made even more explicit later in the book of Hebrews. For instance, consider these passages as we contemplate the "rest" mentioned in Hebrews 4:

These all died in faith, not having received the things promised, but having seen them and greeted them from afar, and having acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth. For people who speak thus make it clear that they are seeking a homeland. If they had been thinking of that land from which they had gone out, they would have had opportunity to return. But as it is, they desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared for them a city. (Hebrews 11:13-16)

Even though the patriarchs were on an earthly pilgrimage, ultimately, they were on a journey that would lead them to a city that was not of this world. They were traveling to a heavenly city prepared for them by God, and it was there, in the city of God, where they would finally find ultimate rest. Hebrews 12 continues to compare the realities of the Old Covenant and the New Covenant in showing how the benefits of the New Covenant are so much greater. In this passage, he again speaks of the place God has prepared for those who have faith in Christ.

But you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to innumerable angels in festal gathering, and to the assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven, and to God, the judge of all, and to the spirits of the righteous made perfect, and to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel. (Hebrews 12:22-24)

According to this passage, the readers who were still alive had somehow already come to the ultimate place of rest, "Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem." But, how could this be, since they, unlike Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, were still alive? By having faith in the Person of rest (Jesus Christ), they were assured of their future entrance into the Place of rest (heaven) that was to come. The author of Hebrews can speak of their future entry into heaven because all that is needful to enter the place of rest had been accomplished by Jesus Christ. Those who had faith in Christ also had received the promised outcome of faith, eternal salvation. Though the Hebrews were not physically in the city of God yet, to a degree, they are. How? Because they had come to "Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant," who guarantees the arrival of all who have faith in Him.

For good news came to us just as to them, but the message they heard did not benefit them, because they were not united by faith with those who listened. (Hebrews 4:2)

The Israelites received good news from God about the future provision of land and rest; however, the good news had no benefit to most of them because they remained in unbelief. Their unbelief led them to die in the desert instead of entering the land of promise, provision, and rest. But what does all of that have to do with the audience of the book of Hebrews? The author compares the good news the Israelites were to believe to the good news (gospel) that the reader had received and was to believe. The Israelites had to believe God to reap the benefits of God's promises. Now a greater good news had come, the saving message of Jesus Christ, and that news had to be believed in for anyone to reap the promises of God that were attached to that good news. The author had already spoken of the news that was even better than what the Israelites of the Exodus had received in Hebrews 2:1- 4

Therefore we must pay much closer attention to what we have heard, lest we drift away from it. For since the message declared by angels proved to be reliable, and every transgression or disobedience received a just retribution, how shall we escape if we neglect such a great salvation? It was declared at first by the Lord, and it was attested to us by those who heard, while God also bore witness by signs and wonders and various miracles and by gifts of the Holy Spirit distributed according to his will. (Hebrews 2:1-4)

The good news of salvation that was declared by Jesus Christ and attested by God the Father and the Holy Spirit had now come, and to neglect this good news was to reject the provision of God for forgiveness and rest. Rest and salvation are tied to the message of the gospel. The good news of provision and rest was of no benefit to the unbelieving Israelites who fell dead and did not enter the Promised Land. Their death served as a typological warning that those who neglected the good news of Christ had no chance of salvation and would receive the wrath of God.

For we who have believed enter that rest, as he has said, "As I swore in my wrath, 'They shall not enter my rest,'" although his works were finished from the foundation of the world. For he has somewhere spoken of the seventh day in this way: "And God rested on the seventh day from all his works." And again in this passage, he said, "They shall not enter my rest." Since therefore it remains for some to enter it, and those who formerly received the good news failed to enter because of disobedience, again he appoints a certain day, "Today," saying through David so long afterward, in the words already quoted, "Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts." (Hebrews 4:3-6)

In this brief section, the author repeats "They shall not enter my rest" two times. He took this quote from Psalm 95, in which God is speaking to the rebellious Israelites during the exodus. God swore that there would be dire consequences to their unbelief, and instead of entering the Promised Land, they would receive the wrath of God. Did God keep His promise? Let's glance back to Numbers and Deuteronomy to find out how God handled the Israelites’ unbelief.

‘But as for you, your dead bodies shall fall in this wilderness. And your children shall be shepherds in the wilderness forty years and shall suffer for your faithlessness, until the last of your dead bodies lies in the wilderness. According to the number of the days in which you spied out the land, forty days, a year for each day, you shall bear your iniquity forty years, and you shall know my displeasure.' I, the LORD, have spoken. Surely this will I do to all this wicked congregation who are gathered together against me: in this wilderness they shall come to a full end, and there they shall die. (Numbers 14:32-35) And the time from our leaving Kadesh-Barnea until we crossed the brook Zered was thirty-eight years, until the entire generation, that is, the men of war, had perished from the camp, as the LORD had sworn to them. For indeed the hand of the LORD was against them, to destroy them from the camp, until they had perished. So as soon as all the men of war had perished and were dead from among the people, the LORD said to me, 'Today you are to cross the border of Moab at Ar. (Deuteronomy 2:14-18)

God certainly kept his word to the Israelites. The unbelieving Israelites fell dead and did not enter God's place of rest, just like He had sworn. However, the author of Hebrews was not quoting this passage because he was concerned about those Israelites who had died without entering God's rest. His concern was with the living who must believe God to enter His rest. What are they to believe? The good news of salvation by grace, through faith in Jesus Christ, carried with it both a greater rest for believers (which the OT rest pointed forward to) and a greater punishment for unbelievers. The author of Hebrews uses the promises of God's rest for the believing Israelites and His wrath to the unbelieving Israelites to reveal even greater promises of rest or wrath regarding God's saving message of the gospel. These truths are seen as we consider how the typological pattern of "rest" found in the Promised Land points to a greater "rest" in Christ. God's place of rest and provision was diametrically opposed to their years in slavery under the rule of the Pharaoh, as can be seen in God's early promises to Moses:

Then the LORD said, "I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt and have heard their cry because of their taskmasters. I know their sufferings, and I have come down to deliver them out of the hand of the Egyptians and to bring them up out of that land to a good and broad land, a land flowing with milk and honey, to the place of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites." (Exodus 3:7-8) "Behold, I send an angel before you to guard you on the way and to bring you to the place that I have prepared. Pay careful attention to him and obey his voice; do not rebel against him, for he will not pardon your transgression, for my name is in him. "But if you carefully obey his voice and do all that I say, then I will be an enemy to your enemies and an adversary to your adversaries. "When my angel goes before you and brings you to the Amorites and the Hittites and the Perizzites and the Canaanites, the Hivites and the Jebusites, and I blot them out, you shall not bow down to their gods nor serve them, nor do as they do, but you shall utterly overthrow them and break their pillars in pieces. You shall serve the LORD your God, and he will bless your bread and your water, and I will take sickness away from among you.” (Exodus 23:20-25)

In this land of promise, God would provide peace, a place of abundant provision (milk, honey, bread, water), protection from enemies, and no sickness. The language that God uses to describe the Promised Land rest should sound familiar to the student of the Bible. For some, it certainly sounds like the final eschatological heaven, and we will get to that in a moment; however, we don't want to miss that God's promised rest to the Israelites rings with similarities to the rest that Adam and Eve experienced at creation before the fall. God had rested from His work, and Adam and Eve were to enjoy the place of God's provision and rest (the Garden of Eden). God rested from His work, and they were to enjoy resting in God.

Thus the heavens and the earth were finished, and all the host of them. And on the seventh day, God finished the work of creation, and he rested on the seventh day from all his work that he had done. So God blessed the seventh day and made it holy, because on it God rested from all his work that he had done in creation. (Genesis 2:1-3)

Unlike the other days of creation, the seventh day was not marked by an "evening and morning.” God rested from His work, and mankind rests in the sufficiency and provision of God. The Garden of Eden is described as a place of unparalleled beauty and rest. However, Adam and Eve did not believe God, believed the lies of Satan, and were banished from the place of God's blessed provision and rest. Now, instead of dining on the delicious fruits that were abundantly grown on the trees of the Garden, they had to get to work. God told them:

“…cursed is the ground because of you; in pain you shall eat of it all the days of your life; thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you… By the sweat of your face you shall eat bread, till you return to the ground, for out of it you were taken; for you are dust, and to dust you shall return." (Genesis 3:17-19)

Because of sin, Adam and Eve were ejected from God's place of rest, and challenging work became the norm. They were also forbidden from returning to the Garden, or they would face the wrath of God. Would mankind ever be able to enter God's place of rest again? The answer is, "Yes!" Look at the words of Christ in these passages and notice how similar the language is to the rest that God had provided for Adam and Eve and the rest that was promised to the Israelites of the exodus.

“Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls.” (Matthew 11:28-29) "Let not your hearts be troubled. Believe in God; believe also in me. In my Father's house are many rooms. If it were not so, would I have told you that I go to prepare a place for you? And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and will take you to myself, that where I am you may be also. And you know the way to where I am going." Thomas said to him, "Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way?" Jesus said to him, "I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me." (John 14:1-6)

These passages reveal the same truth that the author of Hebrews was expressing to his readers when he wrote, "For we who have believed enter that rest."37 There is a future rest connected to belief in Christ in the present. Those who believe in Christ experience rest for their souls now, but of course, that rest will be greater when we arrive in the place of rest that Jesus Christ has prepared for us. The author of Hebrews also makes this point when he tells the believers who were still alive that they had already entered God's rest. How had they entered? By belief in Jesus Christ. The words of Jesus and the words of the author of Hebrews make it clear that to get to the Place of God's rest, one must be on the Path of God's rest through the Person of God's rest: Jesus Christ. Jesus often used Old Testament language of God's provision, rest, and nourishment to point to Himself as the fulfillment of these typological patterns. The emphasis of Jesus' teaching was not about going back to the Garden of Eden, or retaking the Promised Land for Israel to find rest, or making sure we take the Sabbath day off from work. Instead, the focus of His teaching is to believe in Him for the fulfillment of the typological provision and rest. As Jesus said, "I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst." The ultimate need of mankind is not physical food but spiritual food from God, and Jesus Christ is that provision. This entrance into God's rest through Christ is taught by Jesus during His teaching on the Lord's Supper.

And as they were eating, he took bread, and after blessing it broke it and gave it to them, and said, "Take; this is my body." And he took a cup, and when he had given thanks he gave it to them, and they all drank of it. And he said to them, "This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many. Truly, I say to you, I will not drink again of the fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new in the kingdom of God." (Mark 14:22-25)

The Lord's Supper reveals two primary truths. Jesus is the spiritual nourishment that we need now, and it is through Him, we enter a spiritual rest that leads to the complete eschatological rest where we will eat and drink with Him in the final Promised Land: the dwelling place of God. God's place of provision and rest that Adam and Eve briefly enjoyed and that the Israelites were promised but lost due to sin, will one day be fully realized for all who have entered the Sabbath rest of Christ. If we fast forward to the end of the book of Revelation, we can get an even better idea of what it will be like to be in the place of God's provision and rest.

Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away, and the sea was no more. And I saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband. And I heard a loud voice from the throne saying, "Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God. He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away." And he who was seated on the throne said, "Behold, I am making all things new." Also, he said, "Write this down, for these words are trustworthy and true." And he said to me, "It is done! I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end. To the thirsty I will give from the spring of the water of life without payment. The one who conquers will have this heritage, and I will be his God and he will be my son. But as for the cowardly, the faithless, the detestable, as for murderers, the sexually immoral, sorcerers, idolaters, and all liars, their portion will be in the lake that burns with fire and sulfur, which is the second death." (Revelation 21:1-8)

In this passage, we get a glimpse of what it will be like to be in God's place of provision. We also see that just as God told the Israelites and the author of Hebrews told his reader that those who do not believe would not enter God's rest. The unbelievers who continued in sin remain outside of the "promised land." Revelation 22 also brings together the types and patterns of the Garden of Eden, the promises of Israel, and the promises of Christ in a beautiful picture.

Then the angel showed me the river of the water of life, bright as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb through the middle of the street of the city; also, on either side of the river, the tree of life with its twelve kinds of fruit, yielding its fruit each month. The leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations. No longer will there be anything accursed, but the throne of God and of the Lamb will be in it, and his servants will worship him. They will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads. And night will be no more. They will need no light of lamp or sun, for the Lord God will be their light, and they will reign forever and ever. (Revelation 22:1-5)

The end-time vision reveals that the lost place of rest has been restored and improved. The tree of life that was last seen in the Garden of Eden shows up again in the New Creation. Notice that all things accursed are gone, including the thorns, thistles, and the arduous work and sweat required to grow plants. The rest entered through faith in Christ reaches its complete spiritual and physical fulfillment in heaven.

Blessed are those who wash their robes, so that they may have the right to the tree of life and that they may enter the city by the gates. Outside are the dogs and sorcerers and the sexually immoral and murderers and idolaters, and everyone who loves and practices falsehood. "I, Jesus, have sent my angel to testify to you about these things for the churches. I am the root and the descendant of David, the bright morning star." The Spirit and the Bride say, "Come." And let the one who hears say, "Come." And let the one who is thirsty come; let the one who desires take the water of life without price. (Revelation 22:14-17)

These passages help us visualize the ultimate rest we will have and see the One to Whom we go to find that rest.

For if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken of another day later on. So then, there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God, for whoever has entered God's rest has also rested from his works as God did from his. (Hebrews 4:8-10)

After those in the great rebellion had died, God appointed Joshua to lead the people into the Promised Land. Joshua did as God commanded and led the Israelites into the land of promise. Joshua reminded the people that this was the place of rest that God had told Moses about:

"Remember the word that Moses the servant of the LORD commanded you, saying, 'The LORD your God is providing you a place of rest and will give you this land.'" (Joshua 1:13)

However, this place of rest was not without conditions. The people were to continue in belief and obedience. Joshua, like Moses, knew the heart of the people all too well. As Joshua was about to die, he reminded the people of God's faithfulness to His promises and that God would also be faithful to His promise of wrath if they turned against Him.

"And now I am about to go the way of all the earth, and you know in your hearts and souls, all of you, that not one word has failed of all the good things that the LORD your God promised concerning you. All have come to pass for you; not one of them has failed. But just as all the good things that the LORD your God promised concerning you have been fulfilled for you, so the LORD will bring upon you all the evil things, until he has destroyed you from off this good land that the LORD your God has given you, if you transgress the covenant of the LORD your God, which he commanded you, and go and serve other gods and bow down to them. Then the anger of the LORD will be kindled against you, and you shall perish quickly from off the good land that he has given to you." (Joshua 23:14-16)

As in the Garden of Eden, remaining in the place of rest required obedience to God. And like the Garden of Eden, Israel's obedience did not last long. After Joshua died, the Israelites once again rebelled against God.

And all that generation also were gathered to their fathers. And there arose another generation after them who did not know the LORD or the work that he had done for Israel. And the people of Israel did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and served the Baals. And they abandoned the LORD, the God of their fathers, who had brought them out of the land of Egypt. They went after other gods, from among the gods of the peoples who were around them, and bowed down to them. And they provoked the LORD to anger. They abandoned the LORD and served the Baals and the Ashtaroth. So the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he gave them over to plunderers, who plundered them. And he sold them into the hand of their surrounding enemies, so that they could no longer withstand their enemies. Whenever they marched out, the hand of the LORD was against them for harm, as the LORD had warned, and as the LORD had sworn to them. And they were in terrible distress. (Judges 2:10-15)

The provision and rest that God had provided for Israel were lost due to sin. This failure to enter is what Hebrews and the citation of Psalm 95 are alluding to. There must be something greater than the geographical land of promise since it was only a type of something greater. For even after Joshua led them there, they did not rest long. Soon they sinned against God and began to receive His wrath. Yet God's ultimate plan to bring about "rest" continued. The author of Hebrews teaches that the arrival of the Israelites into the land of promise was not the apex of God's plan; that is, He spoke of "another day later on." By citing Psalm 95, he reminded the people that the promise of rest still stood even though the Israelites were in the land. God was teaching them to look forward to a greater rest to come in Christ. The author of Hebrews teaches this truth by emphasizing that God's ultimate rest has now come in Christ. Jesus is greater than Abraham, Moses, and Joshua. For the day that was "later on" has now arrived. Jesus is the greater Joshua that leads His people to the greater Promised land. What does all this talk about God's provision and rest have to do with the Sabbath discussion? Everything. In Hebrews 4:9, we finally see the word "Sabbath." However, even though this is his first use of the word, he lets the reader know that he has been talking about the Sabbath the entire time by writing, "So then, there remains a Sabbath rest." Throughout this section, he has used the language of rest, which is so intrinsically connected to the Sabbath. Yet, he raises the readers' eyes from the types of the Old Testament to the ultimate Sabbath rest that remains for the people of God, which can only be attained by believing in the good news of Jesus Christ. Notice that he never commands the Christians to keep the seventh day holy as was commanded by God to the Israelites. Instead, he tells them that they have entered God's rest and assures them that the rest they have entered through belief in Christ will lead to the ultimate Sabbath. He encourages them to look beyond the types and shadows of the Old Covenant to the absolute and final rest that awaits those who believe the good news. Jesus Christ accomplished all the work of God perfectly by fulfilling God's law.

And this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent. I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do. (John 17:3-4)

Jesus accomplished the work that we could not. He is the only one who ever fulfilled all righteousness, and this He did on our behalf so that all who believe in Him shall be saved from the wrath of God and given the rest of God. Even though we have all sinned and fallen short of the glory of God,38 Jesus, on the other hand, pleased the Father by living in perfect obedience to Him. Christ’s holiness is revealed through His life and resurrection from the dead,39 but also by God the Father’s own words at the baptism of Jesus, as He said, "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased; listen to him."40 There is only one who has lived a perfect life of obedience. There is only One who is qualified to enter the Sabbath rest of God, Jesus Christ. And it is only those who rest in Him that will enter that rest. Summary: According to the author of Hebrews, how does one keep the Sabbath now that the Messiah has come? Is it by working six days and ceasing from work on the seventh? Is it by keeping the Old Covenant Sabbath festivals? Is it by taking every seventh year as a Sabbatical year? No. There is absolutely no mention of the Old Covenant Sabbath regulations because that was for a different covenant. Under the New Covenant, we keep the Sabbath by believing in the Person and work of Jesus Christ for our salvation. As the author of Hebrews says, “We who believe enter that promised rest.” That’s it. There is no special Sabbath day, festival, or year that must be kept; instead, all the focus, as we should expect, is on Jesus Christ. So, if we keep the Sabbath by believing in Christ for salvation under the New Covenant, how then does someone break the Sabbath? Under the Old Covenant, those who did not believe God did not enter the Promised Land to enjoy His provision and rest. The same is true now, but the message to be believed is the gospel, and the promised land is heaven itself. Those who do not believe in the Person and work of Jesus Christ for their salvation remain objects of God’s wrath and will not enjoy His Sabbath Rest.41 Such a person remains in disobedience, remains in unbelief, and will receive the wrath of God. As God says, “They shall not enter my rest.” When God says to rest, He also tells us how to rest. Think back to Numbers when the man was working on the Sabbath. What was his punishment? Death. The man violated the covenant sign and rejected the rest that God had provided for the Israelites. As we raise that incident to its fuller typological trajectory, it could be said that it is still possible to violate the Sabbath and to suffer death as a consequence. However, to violate the Sabbath now would be to work where God says to rest regarding salvation. Anyone who believes that they contribute to their salvation is a Sabbath-breaker under the New Covenant and such a person will die. However, far worse than physical death under the Old Covenant is the spiritual and eternal death for rejecting the Sabbath that Jesus Christ provided.42 Will you enter God's rest or not? The good news is that if you are reading this, then it is not too late. You can know that you will enter God's ultimate place of provision and rest in the future by resting in Christ now. If you want to be in the place of God's rest, then you must be on the Path to God's rest, which is found in the Person of God’s rest: Jesus Christ.

37 Hebrews 4:3

38 Romans 3:23

39 Romans 1:4; Acts 2:24

40 Matthew 3:17

41 John 3:36

42 Revelation 20:11-15

sections.title: CHAPTER 9: WHAT DOES JESUS SAY ABOUT THE SABBATH?
sections.html:
Jesus taught on many issues; however, the keeping of the Old Covenant Sabbath does not appear to be at the top of the list. As we have covered previously, to enter the Sabbath rest of the New Covenant is to believe in Christ. And that is where we see the primary emphasis of Jesus’ teaching. Jesus is the Messiah fulfilling the Old Testament typologies and prophecies so that people may know that He is God’s one and only Savior who will accomplish all the work of redemption. Belief in the true identity of Jesus is central to His teaching, for if they did not believe Him to be who He claimed to be, they would die in their sins, remain an object of God’s wrath, and not enter into eternal rest.43 The emphasis of all of the gospels is overwhelming to present the truth about Jesus Christ so that people may believe and be saved. The Apostle John states this as the purpose for writing his gospel, “but these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name.”44 Mark opens his gospel with Jesus’ proclamation of “The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel.”45 So, with the understanding that ultimate Sabbath rest comes only to those who believe in Him, as the author of Hebrews has stated, “For we who have believed enter that rest,” one could say that Christ taught a great deal on the issue of Sabbath.46 However, if we are only looking at the times when Jesus spoke or taught about the Sabbath of the Mosaic Covenant, it is a different story. When we gather all the times when Jesus mentioned the Sabbath, we have a minuscule amount of Scripture to study. That fact alone speaks loudly that Sabbath regulations were not what Jesus had come to emphasize. Why? Because the Sabbath was a sign of the Old Covenant, and Jesus had come to create the New Covenant and would soon fulfill the typology of the Old Covenant sign of the Sabbath. Therefore, the emphasis of Jesus’ teaching was not on Old Covenant regulations but upon the New Covenant regulation, which was belief in Him. In this chapter, I have compiled the passages where Jesus mentioned the Sabbath or used Sabbath-type language in His teaching. Though many of you may desire to find a simple phrase where Jesus tells everyone to continue or discontinue keeping the Sabbath days, years, and festivals, you will not find such a clear statement. Still, I do believe by the end of this chapter, you will gain much clarity. So, let’s begin.

PASSAGE #1

One Sabbath he was going through the grainfields, and as they made their way, his disciples began to pluck heads of grain. And the Pharisees were saying to him, “Look, why are they doing what is not lawful on the Sabbath?” And he said to them, “Have you never read what David did, when he was in need and was hungry, he and those who were with him: how he entered the house of God, in the time of Abiathar the high priest, and ate the bread of the Presence, which it is not lawful for any but the priests to eat, and also gave it to those who were with him?” And he said to them, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. So the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath.” (Mark 2:23-28)

So, did Jesus break the Sabbath or keep the Sabbath? The Pharisees believed His behavior to be a clear violation of Sabbath regulations. The Pharisees were referencing the rules God gave to Israel when He said, “Six days you shall work, but on the seventh day you shall rest. In plowing time and in harvest you shall rest.”47 In the mind of the Pharisees, plucking heads of grain to eat as Jesus and His disciples walked by the fields was considered harvesting, and harvesting was a violation of the Sabbath. The Pharisees, who were constantly trying to catch Jesus in a trap, believed they had caught Him violating the Sabbath. Does Jesus agree with their accusation? It appears that Jesus and His disciples were not breaking the Sabbath by this small act of eating as they walked. The Pharisees had added many more rules to the Mosaic Covenant that were not originally there but treated them with equal authority. But, instead of Jesus answering the Pharisees with a “Yes, we are breaking the Sabbath.” or, “No, we are not breaking the Sabbath.,” Jesus drew from the Old Testament to remind them of a similar incident involving David. In the story of David, found in 1 Samuel 21, he and his men were famished and desperately needed sustenance. With no place to turn, David hurriedly went by the tabernacle and asked the priest if there was any food there that they could eat. To wrap our minds around the event with David, we must realize that his request was a first of its kind. The tabernacle was not a fast-food restaurant or a food bank for the needy. The Holy Place within the tabernacle did have bread, but that bread was to be eaten only by priests as it was written in Leviticus.

Every Sabbath day Aaron shall arrange it before the LORD regularly; it is from the people of Israel as a covenant forever. And it shall be for Aaron and his sons, and they shall eat it in a holy place, since it is for him a most holy portion out of the LORD’s food offerings, a perpetual due.” (Leviticus 24:8-9)

David’s request and actions regarding the eating of the bread were anomalies. We have no incident ever recorded like this before or after this time. Also, from 1 Samuel 21, we can safely assume this incident happened on the Sabbath like that of Jesus and His disciples.

Now then, what do you have on hand? Give me five loaves of bread, or whatever is here.” And the priest answered David, “I have no common bread on hand, but there is holy bread… So the priest gave him the holy bread, for there was no bread there but the bread of the Presence, which is removed from before the LORD, to be replaced by hot bread on the day it is taken away. (1 Samuel 21:3-4, 6)

By referencing David’s Sabbath day eating holy bread, Jesus pins the Pharisees into a corner where they must decide if David, whom they highly respected, violated the Sabbath or if David’s actions were permissible. The Pharisees knew the story well, and they also knew that no punishment came to David or his men for eating the bread of the Presence on the Sabbath. So, what does that mean for Jesus and his disciples? Jesus compares what He and the disciples are doing to what David and his men did when they needed food. If for some reason it was permissible for David, then Jesus is saying it is also acceptable for Him. But what is that reason? Jesus is certainly advocating for the uniqueness of David’s right to do what others were not allowed to do on the Sabbath and the eating of the bread even though he was not a priest. It is also important to draw out the typologies from the Old Testament text to see that it was permissible for David, for he was in the line of the Messiah who was to come. David was allowed this unusual activity on the Sabbath due to his unique position as the future king of Israel, the one of whom God would make the Davidic Covenant, and of whom the final and everlasting King and High Priest would come. With Jesus, we see the typologies that David represented reach their actual substance or antitype, as Jesus is the supreme King of Israel, the maker and keeper of the New Covenant, and the final High Priest. Not only does Jesus seem to hint at the uniqueness that He shared with David, but He also plainly states that there is something about His identity that puts Him in a class all by Himself. Jesus told them that He is “the Son of Man,” a clearly Messianic title, which also describes one who is both man and God.48 This uniquely qualifies Him so that He answers them by referencing His identity, “So the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath.” The Pharisees raised the rules of the Sabbath above the Lord. However, as God in the flesh, the Sabbath day did not lord over Jesus. He was uniquely qualified to say that He is Lord, even of the Sabbath.

PASSAGE #2

At that time Jesus went through the grainfields on the Sabbath. His disciples were hungry, and they began to pluck heads of grain and to eat. But when the Pharisees saw it, they said to him, “Look, your disciples are doing what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath.” He said to them, “Have you not read what David did when he was hungry, and those who were with him: how he entered the house of God and ate the bread of the Presence, which it was not lawful for him to eat nor for those who were with him, but only for the priests? Or have you not read in the Law how on the Sabbath the priests in the temple profane the Sabbath and are guiltless? I tell you, something greater than the temple is here. And if you had known what this means, ‘I desire mercy, and not sacrifice,’ you would not have condemned the guiltless. For the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath.” (Matthew 12:1-8)

Matthew’s account of the Sabbath confrontation between the Pharisees and Jesus is of the same event as previously mentioned in Mark 2:23-28. However, Matthew includes a couple more details pertaining to the Sabbath discussion. For instance, in Matthew 12:5, Jesus told the Pharisees that priests work in the temple on the Sabbath, yet they are guiltless.
